How the docs separate source repositories, the labs, tools and apps they publish, and the GitHub Projects boards that plan the work.

## Three different things

| Section | Route | What it is | Source of truth |
|---|---|---|---|
| Repositories | `/repos/` | One record per source repository or deployable service. | Markdown in `src/content/repos/` |
| Builds | `/builds/` | The labs, tools and apps people can open and use. | Builds API, snapshotted to `data/builds.json` |
| GitHub Projects | `/boards/` | Planning boards with every issue, pull request and draft item. | GitHub Projects (v2), snapshotted to `data/github-projects.json` |

A repository can publish many builds (for example the tools repository publishes every tool), and a board can track work across several repositories. Repository pages list the builds whose `repository` matches their own.

The old `/projects/` routes redirect to `/repos/`.

## Builds

Builds come from the public builds API:

```bash
curl -X 'GET' \
  'https://api.rjmlaird.co.uk/v1/builds' \
  -H 'accept: application/json'
```

Each build has a `type` of `lab`, `tool` or `app`, and an `id` such as `tools/orbital-calc`. The first segment becomes the route group, so that build lives at `/builds/tools/orbital-calc/`. Builds are grouped using the catalogue's `groups` and ordered by the catalogue's `statuses`.

The Astro build never calls the API. Refresh the snapshot with:

```bash
pnpm sync:builds
```

At the time of writing the API lists apps and tools only. The Labs section is in place and fills in when the API starts returning `type: "lab"` builds.

## GitHub Projects boards

Boards are GitHub Projects (v2) owned by the `rjmlaird` account. Each board page shows the project README, a summary of its single-select fields, a dated timeline, and every item with its labels, assignees, fields and rendered body.

```bash
export GITHUB_TOKEN=ghp_...   # classic PAT: read:project (add repo for private repositories)
pnpm sync:boards
```

Only public projects are written by default (`--include-private` overrides this). Items in private repositories that the token cannot read appear as "Private item" so counts stay honest. Rendered bodies come from GitHub's own renderer, which sanitises the HTML.

## Keeping snapshots fresh

The **Sync builds and boards** workflow refreshes both files every Monday and opens a pull request when anything changes. It needs a `PROJECTS_READ_TOKEN` repository secret for the boards. Review the diff before merging.

# Service documentation template

Copy this structure into a new service record and replace every bracketed instruction. Do not invent URLs, owners, deployment status or dependencies; use `To confirm` where evidence is missing. Keep hostname, visibility and lifecycle aligned with `data/subdomains.json`.

```yaml
---
title: Service name
description: One-sentence purpose and scope.
owner: Team or named role
last_reviewed: YYYY-MM-DD
review_cycle: 6 months
visibility: public # public | restricted | internal
lifecycle: planned # active | planned | reserved | retired
confidence: Unverified
---
```

What the service does, who it serves and what it explicitly does not do.

The checklist for adding a new service or hostname to the rjmlaird.co.uk estate, from justification to documentation, in a single pull request.

A new service touches DNS, security, monitoring and documentation, so it is added in one reviewed change. Nothing here may be skipped; "not applicable" needs a stated reason.

## Requirements

| # | Requirement | Where it is recorded |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | **Justify the hostname.** Meet at least one test in [When a subdomain is justified](../platform/governance/subdomains.md#when-a-subdomain-is-justified); otherwise use a path | ADR or pull request description |
| 2 | **Add a catalogue entry** to `data/subdomains.json` | [Subdomain catalogue](../platform/governance/subdomains.md) |
| 3 | **Write a first-party service page** with one responsibility and its boundaries | `docs/catalogue/first-party/<slug>.md` |
| 4 | **Set visibility and lifecycle explicitly.** Default to restricted for anything that writes, integrates or manages | Catalogue and page front matter |
| 5 | **Decide ownership.** Name who maintains it and where the code lives | Service page |
| 6 | **Decide monitoring.** State whether it has a health check and whether it appears on the status page | Service page; [Observability](../operate/status-and-observability.md) |
| 7 | **Review threats and access.** Cover untrusted input, the shared session cookie, secrets and least privilege | [Security, privacy and access](../platform/governance/security-and-privacy.md) |
| 8 | **Write deployment and rollback notes.** Say how it is released and how it is reversed | [Environments and deployment model](../platform/governance/environments.md) |
| 9 | **Update documentation and status in the same pull request** | This checklist |

## Steps

1. Open the pull request and describe the justification (requirement 1).
2. Add the catalogue record. Use `planned` until the service is verified as running, and set `evidence` honestly.

   ```json title="Catalogue record (illustrative)"
   {
     "slug": "example",
     "hostname": "example.rjmlaird.co.uk",
     "title": "Example",
     "purpose": "One public-safe sentence",
     "classification": "integration",
     "visibility": "restricted",
     "lifecycle": "planned",
     "evidence": "none",
     "documentation": "catalogue/first-party/example.md",
     "publish": true,
     "status": null,
     "health": null,
     "repository": null
   }
   ```

3. Create the service page. Give it `visibility` and `lifecycle` front matter that match the record, and link to shared pages instead of repeating their rules.
4. Run `pnpm run docs:generate`, then `pnpm run docs:check`, and commit the regenerated table.
5. Add the page to `sidebars.ts` in the right group.
6. Build the site and fix any broken link before requesting review.

## Never include

Secrets, credentials, account or binding identifiers, bucket names, internal hostnames, private management or health URLs, and exact access-policy rules.

## After launch

Change `lifecycle` to `active` only when a repository or a check verifies the service, and update the page, the catalogue and the status page together. To retire a service, set `retired`, redirect or remove DNS in the same change, and record the decision.

The review workflow for publishing a dataset through the public reference-data service, including licence, attribution and withdrawal.

This is the proposed workflow for the [data](../catalogue/first-party/data.md) service. Publishing is a deliberate, reviewed act: nothing reaches the public service automatically.

:::info[Status: Proposed]
No dataset has been published through this workflow yet. Adjust it once the service is deployed.
:::

## Before you start

A dataset is eligible only if all of these hold:

- It is public, or you have the right to publish it
- Its licence permits redistribution, and you can state the licence and the attribution it requires
- It contains no personal, customer or private data
- You can name the source and the date it was retrieved

## Workflow

1. **Record the source.** Note where the data came from, its licence, the required attribution and the retrieval date.
2. **Prepare the data.** Clean it reproducibly, with the steps kept in the repository, and define its schema.
3. **Validate.** Check the data against the schema. Reject unexpected fields and missing required values.
4. **Describe it.** Write the metadata: title, description, source, licence, attribution, coverage, update frequency and version.
5. **Review.** A second look at licence, attribution and personal data before anything is merged.
6. **Publish a version.** Release it as a new, immutable version. Never overwrite a published version in place.
7. **Verify.** Fetch the published response and compare it with the source.
8. **Announce.** Update the dataset catalogue and any affected documentation.

## Changing and withdrawing

- A correction is a new version. Keep the previous one available unless it is wrong in a harmful way.
- A breaking schema change is a new major version; see [APIs and integrations](../platform/architecture/apis-and-integrations.md#contract-and-versioning-rules).
- If a dataset must be withdrawn, for example because of a licence or privacy problem, remove it promptly, record why and tell known consumers.

## Never publish

Personal data, customer records, credentials, anything under a licence that forbids redistribution, or data you cannot attribute. See [Security, privacy and access](../platform/governance/security-and-privacy.md#privacy).

Conventions for adding and maintaining Markdown documentation.

## Principles

- Write in British English.
- Start with the reader's goal and prerequisites.
- Separate task instructions from architecture explanation.
- Prefer tested commands and small, copyable examples.
- Label unverified facts and proposed designs explicitly.
- Do not publish secrets, credentials, private operational details or personal data.

## Review metadata

New content defaults to `reviewStatus: needs-review`. Set `reviewStatus: reviewed` only after a maintainer has checked the factual claims, links and steps. Add `lastReviewed` only when that review actually occurs.

## Page template

See the reusable templates in the repository's `templates/` directory. Keep page titles descriptive, URLs stable and cross-links relative to the published documentation site.

Ownership and review expectations for first-party services, integrations and operational documentation.

# Service ownership

Every maintained service should identify a responsible owner or role, a canonical repository, an operational contact route where appropriate, and a review date. If ownership is unknown, state `To confirm`; do not imply that a named individual or team has accepted responsibility.

## Minimum ownership record

- **Accountable owner:** role or team responsible for lifecycle and risk decisions.
- **Technical maintainer:** role responsible for code, configuration and deployment.
- **Documentation reviewer:** owner or delegate who confirms that the page remains accurate.
- **Review cadence:** normally six months for service records, and after material interface, access or deployment changes.
- **Evidence:** repository, deployment evidence or owner confirmation supporting lifecycle claims.

## Review triggers

Review the record when a hostname, owner, data flow, dependency, public interface, security boundary, deployment process or lifecycle changes. Update the canonical registry as part of the same change when it contains the affected fact.

A map of the rjmlaird.co.uk ecosystem, showing what is live, what is being built and what is only planned, plus the principles that govern how the pieces fit together.

This section documents the architecture behind **rjmlaird.co.uk**: the sites, services and infrastructure that make up Ryan Laird's personal, professional and technical web presence. It is written for four readers: the owner and maintainer, future collaborators and contractors, technical readers who want to see how the pieces fit, and non-technical readers who only need a mental model.

:::warning[Read the status labels]
The subdomain list that this section is built around is a **planning model**, not an inventory of running services. Every site and service carries a status label, and anything not yet checked is marked **To confirm**. If a page does not say something is *Live*, do not assume it is.
:::

## How to read this section

### Status labels

| Label | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| **Live** | Serving real traffic today. |
| **In development** | Being built; not yet serving production traffic. |
| **Proposed** | Designed or recommended, but no build has started. |
| **Deferred** | Deliberately postponed until there is a concrete need. Includes exploratory ideas. |
| **Not recommended** | Considered and advised against. Recorded so the question is not reopened by accident. |
| **Deprecated** | Was live; scheduled for removal or already retired. |

### Confidence labels

Each page also carries a `confidence` value in its front matter: **Verified** (checked against a repository or configuration), **Partly verified**, or **Unverified** (from planning notes only). Where a statement is inferred rather than confirmed, it is flagged inline.

## System vision and scope

The ecosystem exists to do five jobs:

1. **Present** a clear professional and personal brand.
2. **Publish** writing, research and astronomy and space communication.
3. **Sell and schedule** services such as tutoring, mentoring and coaching.
4. **Explore** ideas in public through experiments and data pieces.
5. **Run** a small amount of back-office automation behind the scenes.

**In scope:** the public sites, the services and APIs, the documentation site and the infrastructure that connects them.

**Out of scope:** the internals of third-party platforms (GitHub, Stripe, Cal.com, HubSpot, Notion, Zotero). Only the integration points are documented here.

## Guiding principles

1. **Status before subdomain.** Nothing gets a DNS record until it has a catalogue entry with a purpose, a status and an owner.
2. **Paths before subdomains.** Content that shares a build, an audience and a security boundary belongs at a path on the main site. A subdomain must justify itself (see the [subdomain catalogue](governance/subdomains.md#when-a-subdomain-is-justified)).
3. **Static first.** Use a static site wherever possible. Add a Worker only where server-side behaviour is genuinely needed.
4. **Keep public and private surfaces apart.** The public portfolio API and the commercial webhook services are separate systems. Private tools sit behind authentication.
5. **One brand system.** `global.css` on the main site is the single source of truth for the visual identity. Other sites copy from it, never the reverse.
6. **Say what we do not know.** Unknowns are written down as **To confirm**, not papered over.
7. **Prefer reversible, low-cost choices.** This is a one-person operation; every extra moving part is maintenance debt.

## Ecosystem summary

Hostnames, visibility and lifecycle for every service are held in the canonical catalogue and published as the [generated public service catalogue](../catalogue/generated/subdomain-catalogue.md). Each service has a page under [Platform services](../catalogue/first-party/platform-services.md). This section does not repeat them.

## A mental model for non-technical readers

Think of the ecosystem as a shop with four areas:

- **The shop windows** are the public sites: the main site, the docs, the labs and, later, space and research content. Visitors browse them freely.
- **The locked doors** are the sign-in service and the private wiki. Only the owner gets through.
- **The back office** is the set of small services that receive a payment or a booking, record it and update the customer record, without anyone pressing a button.
- **The filing cabinets** are the databases and storage buckets where those services keep their records and files.

## Core technologies

| Technology | Used for | Evidence |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Astro | Main site (`Layout.astro`, `Head.astro`, `global.css`) | Owner-stated |
| Docusaurus 3.10.2 (React 19, Mermaid, local search) | Documentation site | Repository |
| GitHub Pages and GitHub Actions | Hosting and deployment of the docs | Repository |
| pnpm 10 and Node.js 22 (in CI) | Package management and builds | Repository |
| Cloudflare Workers, Hono, KV, D1, R2, Queues, Access | Services and APIs | Owner-stated across several repositories |
| TypeScript, Zod, Vitest, Wrangler | Service code, validation, tests, deployment | Owner-stated |
| GitHub OAuth, Stripe, Cal.com, HubSpot, Notion, Zotero | Third-party integrations | Owner-stated |

How to detect, contain, communicate and learn from an incident affecting the rjmlaird.co.uk estate, written for a single maintainer.

This guide expands the process in [Observability, status and incident response](status-and-observability.md). It is written for one person acting under pressure, so each step says what to do first.

## First ten minutes

1. **Stop the harm.** Roll back a release, disable a route or revoke access. Prefer the quickest reversible action.
2. **Rotate anything exposed.** If a secret may have leaked, rotate it now; see [Secret rotation](runbooks/secret-rotation.md).
3. **Write down what you see.** Time, symptoms and what you changed. You will need this later.
4. **Decide if personal data is involved.** If it may be, treat the incident as serious and go to the section below.

## What kind of incident is it?

| Situation | First action |
| --- | --- |
| Public site down or defaced | Roll back the last deployment; check DNS and hosting |
| Webhook failures or missing payments | Follow [Webhook failures](runbooks/webhook-failures.md) |
| Suspected leaked credential | Rotate it, then review recent use |
| Unexpected access to a restricted service | Revoke the credential or session, then review the access policy |
| Dependency or build compromise | Stop deployments, pin the previous known-good version and review the lockfile |

## Communicate

- If public services are affected, update the [status](../catalogue/first-party/status.md) page once it exists. Say what is affected and when you will next update, not guesses about cause.
- Tell affected customers or partners directly when their data or service is involved.

## Personal data

If personal data may have been lost, exposed or altered, consider your legal duties straight away. Under UK GDPR, a notifiable personal data breach must generally be reported to the Information Commissioner's Office within 72 hours of becoming aware of it. Check the current ICO guidance before relying on this, and seek advice where unsure.

## Review

Within a few days, write a short note:

- What happened, and the timeline
- Impact, and who was told
- Root cause
- What worked, and what slowed you down
- Follow-up actions, each with an owner and a date

If the cause was an architectural weakness, record an [ADR](../platform/decisions/index.md) and update the affected service page.

How rjmlaird.co.uk and its subdomains are resolved, which parts of the DNS setup are confirmed, and the rules for adding or retiring a subdomain.

The domain architecture of rjmlaird.co.uk is intended to keep DNS small, predictable and easy to audit. This page records what is known about the current setup, what is inferred, and the rules that decide whether a new subdomain gets created. :::info[Status: Draft] Only the docs hostname is verified from a repository. The registrar and authoritative nameservers are **not yet documented**. Treat everything marked *inferred* or *To confirm* as unchecked. ::: ## Global DNS strategy | Question | Answer | Basis | | --- | --- | --- | | Who is the registrar? | To confirm | Not recorded | | Who runs the authoritative nameservers? | Probably Cloudflare | **Inferred**: the auth Worker uses a Custom Domain route, which requires the zone's DNS to be managed by Cloudflare | | How does `docs` resolve? | CNAME to GitHub Pages | Repository README and `static/CNAME` | | How do Worker hostnames resolve? | Cloudflare Worker Custom Domains | Owner-stated for `auth` and `hooks` | | Is there a wildcard DNS record? | To confirm | Not recorded | | Is DNSSEC enabled? | To confirm | Not recorded | The practical consequence is a **split hosting model**. Static content may live on GitHub Pages or another static host, while services live on Cloudflare Workers. DNS is the one place that holds the whole picture together, which is why it deserves its own documentation. ## Root domain and apex routing The planning inventory names `www.rjmlaird.co.uk` as the canonical web presence and `rjmlaird.co.uk` as the root domain. **Proposed rule:** pick one canonical host and permanently redirect (301) the other to it. Following the inventory, that means: - `https://www.rjmlaird.co.uk` serves the site. - `https://rjmlaird.co.uk` redirects to `https://www.rjmlaird.co.uk`, preserving the path. **Trade-offs.** Using `www` as canonical is the traditional choice and keeps the apex record simple. Using the apex as canonical gives shorter URLs and matches how the site is already referred to elsewhere. Either works; what matters is choosing one and applying it everywhere, including sitemaps, `rel="canonical"` tags and cookie scope. :::note[To confirm / technical debt] The docs site currently links to the **apex** (`https://rjmlaird.co.uk`) in its navbar and footer, which contradicts the inventory's choice of `www` as canonical. Decide which host is canonical, then update `docusaurus.config.ts` to match. Record the decision in an [ADR](decisions/index.md). ::: ## Subdomain resolution rules 1. **Lowercase, single-label, one purpose.** For example `docs`, never `docs-and-guides`. The domain architecture of rjmlaird.co.uk is intended to keep DNS small, predictable and easy to audit. This page records what is known about the current setup, what is inferred, and the rules that decide whether a new subdomain gets created.

:::info[Status: Draft] Only the docs hostname is verified from a repository. The registrar and authoritative nameservers are not yet documented. Treat everything marked inferred or To confirm as unchecked. :::

Global DNS strategy

QuestionAnswerBasis
Who is the registrar?To confirmNot recorded
Who runs the authoritative nameservers?Probably CloudflareInferred: the auth Worker uses a Custom Domain route, which requires the zone’s DNS to be managed by Cloudflare
How does docs resolve?CNAME to GitHub PagesRepository README and static/CNAME
How do Worker hostnames resolve?Cloudflare Worker Custom DomainsOwner-stated for auth and hooks
Is there a wildcard DNS record?To confirmNot recorded
Is DNSSEC enabled?To confirmNot recorded

The practical consequence is a split hosting model. Static content may live on GitHub Pages or another static host, while services live on Cloudflare Workers. DNS is the one place that holds the whole picture together, which is why it deserves its own documentation.

Root domain and apex routing

The planning inventory names www.rjmlaird.co.uk as the canonical web presence and rjmlaird.co.uk as the root domain.

Proposed rule: pick one canonical host and permanently redirect (301) the other to it. Following the inventory, that means:

  • https://www.rjmlaird.co.uk serves the site.
  • https://rjmlaird.co.uk redirects to https://www.rjmlaird.co.uk, preserving the path.

Trade-offs. Using www as canonical is the traditional choice and keeps the apex record simple. Using the apex as canonical gives shorter URLs and matches how the site is already referred to elsewhere. Either works; what matters is choosing one and applying it everywhere, including sitemaps, rel="canonical" tags and cookie scope.

:::note[To confirm / technical debt] The docs site currently links to the apex (https://rjmlaird.co.uk) in its navbar and footer, which contradicts the inventory’s choice of www as canonical. Decide which host is canonical, then update docusaurus.config.ts to match. Record the decision in an ADR. :::

Subdomain resolution rules

  1. Lowercase, single-label, one purpose. For example docs, never docs-and-guides. Names describe a function, not a vendor.
  2. No subdomain without a catalogue entry. Every record must correspond to a row in the subdomain catalogue with a status and an owner.
  3. No wildcard DNS record. A wildcard hides typos and widens the takeover surface. (The shared session cookie is scoped to *.rjmlaird.co.uk, but that is a cookie setting, not a DNS record.)
  4. Remove records when retiring a service. A CNAME pointing at a deleted GitHub Pages site or an abandoned SaaS tenant can be claimed by someone else. Delete the DNS record in the same change that retires the service.
  5. Prefer redirects to new hostnames. A retired subdomain should redirect to its path replacement for as long as old links are likely to exist, then be removed.

How the health of the ecosystem is monitored, how status is communicated and what to do when something breaks. Mostly proposed; little is confirmed.

Good observability for a small ecosystem means knowing quickly that something is broken, finding out why, and telling the right people. Almost none of that is documented as in place, so this page is mainly a proposal and a list of questions.

:::info[Status: Proposed]
No monitoring, error-tracking, analytics or status tooling is confirmed. Candidate tools below are options to evaluate, not decisions.
:::

## What exists today

| Capability | Status |
| --- | --- |
| Build failure notification for the docs | GitHub Actions run status only |
| Worker logs and metrics | Cloudflare provides these for Workers. The services Workers emit structured JSON logs with request, correlation and event identifiers and redact emails and tokens; where the logs are read is to confirm |
| Uptime monitoring | To confirm |
| Error tracking | To confirm |
| Public status page | Proposed (`status`); no confirmed implementation |
| Analytics | To confirm |

## Proposed approach

### Health checks

Each service should offer one cheap endpoint that returns whether it is healthy. The API template in these docs already sketches `GET /status` returning `ok` and `version`; adopt a consistent form such as `GET /v1/status` across every Worker.

Each catalogue entry says whether a service is public. Only public services may publish a health URL, and restricted services' checks stay private. Never list internal health or monitoring URLs in public documentation.

### Logging

- Log events, not secrets or personal data.
- Include a request or event identifier so a failed webhook can be traced from provider to consumer.
- Keep retention short unless a legal or business reason says otherwise.

### Status communication

Host any public status page **outside** the infrastructure it reports on. A status page that goes down with the thing it monitors tells nobody anything. The page is curated: it reports a service state, drawn from the catalogue's public services, not raw metrics or logs. See [status](../catalogue/first-party/status.md).

### Alerting

Alert on a small number of things you would act on at once: webhook failures, a failed scheduled sync, and the public sites being unreachable. Too many alerts will be ignored.

## Incident response

The full guide is [Incident response](incident-response.md). A pragmatic process for a single maintainer:

1. **Detect.** An alert, a failed workflow run or a report.
2. **Assess.** What is affected, and is any personal data involved?
3. **Contain.** Roll back, disable a route or rotate a secret.
4. **Communicate.** Update the status page if public services are affected. If personal data may have been exposed, consider legal reporting duties promptly.
5. **Fix and verify.**
6. **Review.** Write a short note. If the cause was an architectural weakness, record an [ADR](../platform/decisions/index.md).

## To confirm

1. Is any uptime monitoring running?
2. Are Cloudflare Worker logs enabled, and where are they read?
3. Who is notified when a scheduled job fails?
4. Is there any analytics on the public sites, and if so which?

The sequence in which planned parts of the rjmlaird.co.uk ecosystem should be built or documented, the decisions still open and where decisions are recorded.

This roadmap orders the work so that foundations come before features. It deliberately uses **Now, Next, Later and Defer** instead of dates: for a one-person project, sequence matters more than a calendar.

## Roadmap

### Now

| Item | Why now |
| --- | --- |
| Document the confirmed foundation (this section) | Maintainers need one accurate description |
| Deploy `auth` | Other private tools depend on it |
| Ship the `hooks` MVP | Payment and booking events are the revenue-critical automation |
| Decide the canonical host (apex or `www`) | Affects every canonical link, sitemap and cookie |
| Fix the brand token sync between the main site and the docs | Known gap with a known fix |

### Next

| Item | Why next |
| --- | --- |
| Build the wiki MVP | Architecture is already agreed |
| Confirm and publish `api` | Gives the portfolio a stable public interface |
| Establish `research` | Depends on the Zotero ingest pipeline |
| Establish `space` | Content hub, once there is content |
| Replace the template pages in `getting-started`, `api` and `guides` | They currently describe an example project |

### Later

| Item | Condition |
| --- | --- |
| Status page | Once there are services worth reporting on |
| Single asset host | Once media outgrows the site builds |
| Preview deployments for docs | When more than one contributor is involved |

### Deferred or not recommended

| Item | Position |
| --- | --- |
| `dev`, `courses`, `dashboards`, `mcp` | Defer until a concrete need appears |
| `home`, `sandbox`, `dam`, `upload`, `app` | Not recommended |
| Merging 16 content subdomains into paths | Decide in an ADR, then implement as the sites are built |

## Open decisions

1. Canonical host: apex or `www`.
2. Whether `cv` and `research` stay separate from the main site.
3. How brand tokens are shared between sites.
4. Which newsletter and booking providers, and whether their custom domains are needed.
5. Whether the architecture docs are included in versioned snapshots.

## Decision log

Decisions are recorded as ADRs. See the [ADR index](decisions/index.md) for the full list and the backlog of decisions still to be written down.

Shared terms used throughout the RJM Laird platform documentation.

# Terminology

| Term | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| **First-party service** | A capability operated as part of the RJM Laird platform, with an owner, purpose, interfaces, dependencies and operational considerations. |
| **External integration** | A vendor, product or connected system on which a first-party service depends. |
| **Canonical source** | The one maintained source from which repeated facts or generated output are derived. |
| **ADR** | Architecture Decision Record: a durable record of a significant decision, its context, options and consequences. |
| **Runbook** | A concrete procedure for a routine operational task, incident or failure mode. |
| **Contract** | A versioned or otherwise explicit interface definition for HTTP APIs, events, webhooks or data. |
| **Lifecycle** | The current state of a service or hostname, such as planned, active, reserved or retired. |
| **Evidence** | The basis for a lifecycle claim; a catalogue row alone is not evidence of deployment. |
| **Public** | Intended to be accessible without an account. Do not infer that all operational details are safe to publish. |
| **Restricted** | Intended for authenticated, approved or otherwise limited access. Never publish credentials or private endpoints. |
| **Generated document** | Output derived from a canonical data source and generator; update the source and regenerate rather than editing the output. |

Use British English and define specialist abbreviations on first use unless they are common in the relevant technical context.

# Contributor quickstart

## 1. Install dependencies

Use the pinned package manager and lockfile so local and CI environments are consistent.

```bash
corepack enable
pnpm install --frozen-lockfile
```

## 2. Start the local site

```bash
pnpm start
```

Open the local URL printed by Docusaurus. Stop the server with `Ctrl+C` when finished.

## 3. Edit the canonical page

Choose the page's home based on its purpose: cross-cutting design belongs in `docs/platform/`, first-party and vendor records in `docs/catalogue/`, implementation contracts in `docs/build/`, and procedures in `docs/operate/`. Update a canonical source rather than duplicating repeated facts.

## 4. Validate before review

```bash
pnpm run docs:generate
pnpm run docs:check
pnpm run typecheck
pnpm run build
```

If you did not change `data/subdomains.json`, the generation command should not change the generated catalogue. Never edit generated output by hand.

The D1 tables used by the services system, their key constraints and status values, and what is deliberately never stored.

D1 is private storage, never exposed over HTTP. This page gathers what the other documents say about its tables. It is a summary, not the schema.

:::note[Authoritative schema]
The full column definitions live in the repository's `migrations/` directory. Only facts stated elsewhere in the documentation appear here.
:::

## Tables

| Table | Purpose | Key facts |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `webhook_events` | Ledger of every verified provider event | Unique on `(provider, provider_event_id)`. `processing_status` is `received`, `processed` or `failed`. A processed event is skipped. |
| `bookings` | Cal.com bookings | `status = 'cancelled'` is terminal by design. |
| `payments` | One row per payment | A Checkout Session and its PaymentIntent resolve to the same row. `booking_id` is reserved for future reconciliation. |
| `provider_links` | Maps internal records to provider ids | Stores the HubSpot id against a booking or payment. |
| `delivery_workflows` | Client-delivery workflow state | `workflow_key` is unique. Status moves `pending` to `started` or `failed`. |

Business state and the "processed" mark for an event are written in one `D1.batch()` transaction. See [Delivery semantics](../../catalogue/first-party/service-delivery-architecture.md#delivery-semantics).

## Never stored

- Card data
- Raw provider payloads
- Email addresses (they travel only in queue messages)
- Secrets or tokens (logs redact them too)

## Useful queries

The queries for finding stuck events are in the [webhook failures runbook](../../operate/runbooks/webhook-failures.md#triage).

- [Internal events](events.md)

The Zod-defined event envelope, the event types carried on the queues, money and CRM rules, and the versioning policy for backward compatibility.

After a webhook is verified, only the minimum fields are mapped into an internal event. Provider payloads are external input and are never passed on as they are. The source of truth is `packages/service-contracts/src/events.ts` (Zod); `eventJsonSchema()` exports it as JSON Schema.

## Envelope

| Field | Description |
| --- | --- |
| `eventId` | `evt_` followed by 32 hex characters, deterministic from provider, source id and type |
| `correlationId` | UUID minted at ingress and carried through every derived event |
| `occurredAt` | ISO 8601, UTC |
| `schemaVersion` | `1` |
| `source` | `{ provider, eventId, payloadVersion? }` |
| `type` | One of the types below |
| `payload` | Type-specific body |

## Event types

| Type | Carried on |
| --- | --- |
| `payment.confirmed.v1` | `service-events` |
| `payment.failed.v1` | `service-events` |
| `booking.created.v1` | `service-events` |
| `booking.cancelled.v1` | `service-events` |
| `crm.upsert-contact.v1` | `crm-sync-jobs` |
| `client-delivery.start.v1` | `client-delivery-jobs` (inferred from the queue name) |

## Rules

- Money is `amountMinor` (a non-negative integer) plus a lowercase ISO 4217 `currency`. Never use floats.
- CRM jobs must declare a `lawfulBasis`.
- Consumers re-validate every message against the schema, including across the RPC hop to `calcom-consumer`.

## Backward compatibility

- The version is part of the type name. Additive, optional fields stay in `v1`.
- A breaking change creates a `v2` type. Producers emit both versions until every consumer handles `v2`, then `v1` is removed.
- Consumers send unknown types to the DLQ rather than dropping them silently.

How the client-delivery consumer records workflows and hands new clients over, and how to add a real handover adapter.

`client-delivery` is a private consumer of the `client-delivery-jobs` queue. For each `workflowKey` it stores a durable workflow row in D1 (`pending`, then `started` or `failed`) and calls a `HandoverAdapter`.

## Behaviour

- Delivery starts only on the first transition of a payment to `succeeded`.
- `delivery_workflows.workflow_key` is unique, so duplicate messages collapse into one workflow.
- Messages that exhaust their retries go to `client-delivery-jobs-dlq`.
- The default adapter only logs. No client is actually handed over until an adapter is added.

## Adding an adapter

To connect Notion, OpenProject or email:

1. Implement `HandoverAdapter` in `src/adapters.ts`.
2. Return it from `selectAdapter`.
3. Add that provider's secret to this Worker only.

## To confirm

:::note[To confirm]
1. Which adapter comes first.
2. How a workflow stuck in `failed` is retried or closed.
:::

This page lists names only, never values. Set secrets with `wrangler secret put`, which reads from standard input. Never paste a secret into a ticket, a chat or a repository.

```bash title="Setting a secret"
wrangler secret put <NAME> --config <path/to/wrangler.jsonc> [--env staging]
```

## Secrets and variables by Worker

| Worker | Name | Kind | Purpose |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `service-hooks` | `STRIPE_WEBHOOK_SECRET` | Secret | `whsec_…`; one per endpoint and environment |
| `service-hooks` | `CALCOM_WEBHOOK_SECRET` | Secret | HMAC secret for Cal.com payloads |
| `service-hooks` | `HUBSPOT_CLIENT_SECRET` | Secret | Verifies HubSpot v3 signatures |
| `service-hooks` | `ENVIRONMENT` | Variable | `production` disables unsigned mode |
| `service-hooks` | `CALCOM_ALLOW_UNSIGNED` | Variable | Non-production only; permits unsigned Cal.com payloads |
| `billing` | `STRIPE_SECRET_KEY` | Secret | Restricted key: Checkout Sessions write |
| `billing` | `STRIPE_PRICE_*` | Secret | Price IDs, for example `STRIPE_PRICE_STRATEGY_SESSION` and `STRIPE_PRICE_SPACE_COMMS_AUDIT`. Not sensitive, but validated as the purchase allowlist |
| `billing` | `CHECKOUT_*` | Variable | Three redirect URLs (names to confirm) |
| `booking` | `CALCOM_BASE_URL` | Variable | Base URL for Cal.com handoff |
| `hubspot-sync` | `HUBSPOT_ACCESS_TOKEN` | Secret | Private app token, contacts read and write only |

- **Routes:** zone and route patterns for the `hooks`, `booking` and `billing` subdomains.

The public HTTP endpoints of the booking, billing and webhook Workers, with request and response shapes, status codes and error format.

This page lists every HTTP route the services system exposes. Anything not listed returns `404`. Internal events are covered separately in [Internal events](events.md).

## Conventions

- Errors are JSON of the form `{ "error": "<stable_code>", "requestId": "..." }`. They never contain internals.
- Every JSON response carries security headers and an `X-Request-Id` header.
- Public Workers use route and method allow-lists, explicit CORS origins, strict Zod bodies and rate limiting.

## Webhook ingress (`service-hooks`)

Bodies are the provider's raw payloads. Signature verification happens before anything is parsed.

| Method and path | Provider | Signature header | Details |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `POST /v1/webhooks/stripe` | Stripe | `Stripe-Signature` | [Stripe](../../catalogue/external-integrations/stripe.md) |
| `POST /v1/webhooks/calcom` | Cal.com | `X-Cal-Signature-256` | [Cal.com](../../catalogue/external-integrations/calcom.md) |
| `POST /v1/webhooks/hubspot` | HubSpot | `X-HubSpot-Signature-v3` | [HubSpot](../../catalogue/external-integrations/hubspot.md#inbound-webhook-route) |

| Status | Meaning | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `200` | `{ "received": true }`, or `{ "received": true, "ignored": true }` for a verified event that is deliberately not processed | Event accepted |
| `400` | Invalid signature or payload (`invalid_signature` for signature failures) | Failures return a generic body |
| `413` | Body too large | Body exceeds the size limit |
| `500` | Secret missing for this environment (`webhook_not_configured`) | Not configured, not a provider fault |
| `503` | Enqueue failed (`temporarily_unavailable`) | The provider retries, so watch rather than act |

## Booking (`booking`)

| Method and path | Purpose |
| --- | --- |
| `GET /v1/services` | List the bookable services. |
| `POST /v1/booking-intents` | Create a booking intent. |

```json title="POST /v1/booking-intents (request body)"
{ "serviceId": "<service id>", "timezone": "<optional timezone>" }
```

## Billing (`billing`)

| Method and path | Purpose |
| --- | --- |
| `POST /v1/checkout-sessions` | Create a Stripe Checkout Session for a service and intent. |
| `POST /v1/customer-portal-sessions` | Not implemented. Always returns `501`. |

```json title="POST /v1/checkout-sessions (request and response)"
{ "serviceId": "<service id>", "intentId": "<intent id>" }
```

```json title="Response"
{ "sessionId": "<Stripe session id>", "url": "<Checkout URL>" }
```

`serviceId` must resolve to a configured Stripe Price; see the [configuration reference](service-configuration.md).

How Cal.com booking webhooks are configured and verified for the services system, including the values to enter, the assumptions made and known gaps.

Cal.com handles scheduling. When a booking is created or cancelled, Cal.com calls `service-hooks`, which verifies the signature and queues a normalised event.

## Implementation assumptions

- Cal.com signs the **raw body** with HMAC-SHA256 using the webhook's secret and sends the hex digest in `X-Cal-Signature-256`. `verifyCalcomSignature` (`apps/service-hooks/src/calcom.ts`) implements exactly this and nothing else.
- Cal.com sends **no timestamp**, so replay protection relies on idempotency, not on a time window.
- Payloads carry no event id. The source event id is `<triggerEvent>:<booking uid>`.
- A rescheduled booking gets a new uid. `BOOKING_RESCHEDULED` is acknowledged and ignored in the MVP.

## Failure behaviour

| Condition | Response |
| --- | --- |
| Secret missing in production | `500 webhook_not_configured` |
| Signature missing or wrong | `400` |
| Unsigned mode | Allowed only when `ENVIRONMENT` is not `production` **and** `CALCOM_ALLOW_UNSIGNED` is `true` |

## Setup

In Cal.com, go to Settings, then Developer, then Webhooks, then New, and enter:

| Field | Value |
| --- | --- |
| Subscriber URL | `https://hooks.rjmlaird.co.uk/v1/webhooks/calcom` |
| Secret | The value stored as `CALCOM_WEBHOOK_SECRET` |
| Event triggers | Booking Created and Booking Cancelled only |
| Payload template | Default (leave empty) |
| Active | On, after the secret is set on the Worker |

Also set `CALCOM_BASE_URL` on the `booking` Worker, and create event types whose slugs match `calcomSlug` in `packages/service-contracts/src/services.ts`.

:::warning[Use the default payload template]
Custom templates change the body and fail validation.
:::

## Testing

Unit tests sign synthetic payloads (`apps/service-hooks/test/webhooks.test.ts`). For staging, use Cal.com's "Ping test" and a throwaway booking, then check `webhook_events` in the staging D1 database.

## To confirm

:::note[To confirm]
1. That the production webhook has a secret and uses the default payload template.
2. Whether Cal.com retries failed deliveries. The runbooks assume it does, but the integration notes do not say so. If it does not, a `503` or a rotation gap loses a booking until reconciled by hand.
3. Reschedule handling. Only two triggers are subscribed, so `BOOKING_RESCHEDULED` never reaches the Worker. A rescheduled booking may therefore leave a stale row and an outdated HubSpot status.
:::

How contacts are synchronised one way to HubSpot, the private app and properties required, retry behaviour and data minimisation rules.

HubSpot remains the CRM authority. `hubspot-sync` pushes contacts one way and never reads HubSpot state back.

## Access

1. Create a **private app** with only `crm.objects.contacts.read` and `crm.objects.contacts.write`.
2. Store its token as `HUBSPOT_ACCESS_TOKEN` on `hubspot-sync` only.
3. Create two custom contact properties (single-line text): `rjm_booking_status` and `rjm_lifecycle_note`. To use different internal names, set `HUBSPOT_PROP_BOOKING_STATUS` and `HUBSPOT_PROP_LIFECYCLE_NOTE`.

Create the properties before the first job runs.

## Mapping

A `crm.upsert-contact.v1` job maps to a contact like this. Nothing else is sent.

| Job field | HubSpot property |
| --- | --- |
| `email` (lower-cased; the match key) | `email` |
| First name | `firstname` |
| Last name | `lastname` |
| Booking status | `rjm_booking_status` |
| Lifecycle note | `rjm_lifecycle_note` |

A job without a valid email or a `lawfulBasis` is rejected by the contract and dead-lettered.

**Flow:** search by email, then `PATCH` if found or `POST` to create. If HubSpot returns an id, it is saved in `provider_links` against the booking or payment.

## Retries

| Condition | Behaviour |
| --- | --- |
| `429` | Retry, honouring `Retry-After` |
| `409`, `5xx`, network error | Retry |
| Missing token (operator error) | Retry |
| Permanent `4xx` (bad scope, invalid property) | Straight to `crm-sync-jobs-dlq` |

Backoff runs from 30 seconds to 10 minutes, with at most 5 deliveries before the message goes to the DLQ.

## Inbound webhook route

`POST /v1/webhooks/hubspot` verifies the v3 signature (`X-HubSpot-Signature-v3`, with a 5-minute timestamp window, using `HUBSPOT_CLIENT_SECRET`) and acknowledges. In the MVP it enqueues nothing.

:::note[To confirm]
Only configure a HubSpot webhook subscription once an inbound use case exists.
:::

## Data minimisation

- Emails travel only in queue messages. They are never written to D1 or to logs (key-based and pattern-based redaction).
- Each job declares its lawful basis. The MVP uses `contract` for people who book or pay.
- Logs never contain emails or tokens.

:::note[To confirm]
1. A deletion path (HubSpot GDPR delete) in the data-subject request process.
2. How long queue messages, including DLQ messages that carry emails, are retained. Emails are absent from D1, but they persist in queues until retention expires.
3. Which HubSpot app supplies `HUBSPOT_CLIENT_SECRET`, given that the contact sync uses a private app.
:::

Step-by-step rotation of the Stripe, Cal.com and HubSpot credentials used by the services Workers, including the zero-downtime Stripe procedure.

Rotate a credential on a schedule you choose, and immediately on any suspicion of leakage.

:::warning[Never paste secrets]
Do not put secrets in tickets or chat. Use `wrangler secret put`, which reads from standard input.
:::

Secret names and the Worker that holds each one are in the [configuration reference](../../build/reference/service-configuration.md).

## Stripe webhook secret (zero-downtime)

1. In the Dashboard, open the endpoint and choose **Roll secret**. Pick a delay for the old secret (for example 24 hours). Stripe signs with both secrets during that window, so the header carries two `v1` values.
2. Set the new value on the Worker. The verifier accepts any matching `v1`.

   ```bash title="Set the new secret"
   wrangler secret put STRIPE_WEBHOOK_SECRET --config apps/service-hooks/wrangler.jsonc [--env staging]
   ```

3. Confirm a fresh test event returns `200`. The old secret then expires on its own.

## Cal.com webhook secret

Cal.com has a single secret and no overlap window, so some risk of a gap is unavoidable. Choose one path.

**Path A: accept a few `400` responses.** Set the new `CALCOM_WEBHOOK_SECRET` on the Worker first, then change the secret in Cal.com.

**Path B: avoid `400` responses.**

1. Pause the webhook in Cal.com.
2. Set the new secret in Cal.com.
3. Set `CALCOM_WEBHOOK_SECRET` on the Worker.
4. Re-enable the webhook.
5. Check `webhook_events`.

Either way, compare Cal.com's booking list with `webhook_events` afterwards. Bookings made while the webhook was paused or failing may not have been delivered.

## Stripe API key (billing)

1. Create a new **restricted** key (Checkout Sessions write).
2. Set it with `wrangler secret put STRIPE_SECRET_KEY`.
3. Test checkout in staging.
4. Delete the old key.

Price IDs are not secret, but they are validated as an allowlist. To change one, create a new Price and update the matching `STRIPE_PRICE_*` value.

## HubSpot token and client secret

**Access token:**

1. Create a new private-app token with the same minimal scopes.
2. Set it on `hubspot-sync`.

   ```bash title="Set the new token"
   wrangler secret put HUBSPOT_ACCESS_TOKEN --config workers/hubspot-sync/wrangler.jsonc
   ```

3. Watch one job succeed.
4. Revoke the old token.

**Client secret (`HUBSPOT_CLIENT_SECRET`):** rotate it in the app settings, then update the Worker.

## After any rotation

- Check logs for new `signature rejected` or `403` spikes.
- Confirm `webhook_events` keeps moving.
- Record the date.

## To confirm

:::note[To confirm]
Where rotation dates are recorded, and the rotation interval.
:::

How Stripe Checkout and webhooks are set up for the services system, how signatures are verified, how duplicates are handled and how to recover missed events.

Stripe handles payment. The `billing` Worker creates Checkout Sessions, and `service-hooks` receives Stripe's webhooks. The signed webhook is the only proof of payment.

## Events handled

Subscribe the endpoint to exactly these three events.

| Event | Handling |
| --- | --- |
| `checkout.session.completed` | Recorded when `payment_status` is `paid`. Otherwise (delayed payment methods) acknowledged and ignored. |
| `payment_intent.succeeded` | Recorded. Maps to the same `payments` row as the session. |
| `payment_intent.payment_failed` | Recorded as a failed payment. |

## Setup

1. In the Dashboard (Developers, then Webhooks), add the endpoint `https://hooks.rjmlaird.co.uk/v1/webhooks/stripe`. For staging, use the staging host in test mode.
2. Select the three events above and no others.
3. Reveal the signing secret and store it on `service-hooks`:

   ```bash title="Set the webhook secret"
   wrangler secret put STRIPE_WEBHOOK_SECRET --config apps/service-hooks/wrangler.jsonc
   ```

4. Create a Price for each paid service. Set the matching `STRIPE_PRICE_*` secret on `billing`. These Price IDs are the purchase allowlist.
5. Create a restricted API key with Checkout Sessions write access and store it as `STRIPE_SECRET_KEY` on `billing`.

Secret names are listed in the [configuration reference](../../build/reference/service-configuration.md).

## Verification

`service-hooks` reads the raw body once, as text, and checks the `Stripe-Signature` header (`t=…,v1=…`):

- HMAC-SHA256 over `${t}.${rawBody}`, using Web Crypto and the endpoint's signing secret.
- Any `v1` value may match, which supports secret rotation.
- A 5-minute timestamp tolerance.
- JSON is parsed only after verification. Failures return a generic `400`.

:::note[To confirm / technical debt]
This is a hand-rolled implementation of Stripe's documented scheme, chosen to keep the bundle small. It ignores the older `v0` scheme. To use the SDK instead, call `Stripe.createSubtleCryptoProvider()` with `constructEventAsync`. Consider recording the choice as an ADR.
:::

## Idempotency

Stripe retries and duplicates events, so there are two layers of protection.

- **Event level:** `webhook_events` is unique on `(provider, provider_event_id)`.
- **Business level:** the Checkout Session and its PaymentIntent resolve to one `payments` row, and delivery starts once.
- **Session creation:** `billing` sends `Idempotency-Key: checkout:<serviceId>:<intentId>`.

A browser success redirect is never proof of payment.

## Testing

Use test keys, a separate staging endpoint and `stripe listen` locally. Never mix live and test secrets in one environment. Use only Stripe's documented test card numbers.

## Recovery

To recover a missed event, open the endpoint in the Dashboard and resend the event. Resending is safe because duplicates are skipped. If a payment completed while ingress was down, resend `checkout.session.completed`. Check for refunds and disputes first; see [When not to replay](../../operate/runbooks/webhook-failures.md#when-not-to-replay).

1. The names of the three `CHECKOUT_*` URL settings and where each is set.
2. How payments from manually sent payment links are reconciled (see [Customer journeys](../first-party/customer-journeys.md#to-confirm)).
:::

How to find, diagnose and safely replay failed or missed webhook events in the services system, and when not to replay them.

Use this runbook when a provider reports failed deliveries, a booking or payment is missing, or a DLQ is growing. Work through triage, decide whether replay is safe, then replay in the least invasive way.

## Triage

Check these four places in order.

1. **Provider dashboard.** Delivery attempts and response codes (Stripe, Cal.com).
2. **Worker logs.** Structured JSON, searchable by `requestId`, `correlationId` and `eventId`. Emails and tokens are redacted.

   ```bash title="Live logs"
   wrangler tail --config apps/service-hooks/wrangler.jsonc
   ```

3. **D1.** Look for events that never finished.

   ```sql title="Event status overview"
   SELECT processing_status, COUNT(*) FROM webhook_events GROUP BY 1;
   ```

   ```sql title="Events stuck for more than 15 minutes"
   SELECT * FROM webhook_events
    WHERE processing_status != 'processed'
      AND received_at < datetime('now', '-15 minutes');
   ```

   `received` for a long time means a crashed or retrying attempt. `failed` means the system gave up.

4. **Dead-letter queues.** `service-events-dlq`, `crm-sync-jobs-dlq` and `client-delivery-jobs-dlq`. Messages are kept only for the queue retention period, so triage promptly.

## Symptoms and likely causes

| Symptom | Likely cause |
| --- | --- |
| Provider shows `400 invalid_signature` | Wrong or rotated secret, body modified by a proxy, or clock skew (Stripe) |
| `500 webhook_not_configured` | Secret not set for that environment |
| `503 temporarily_unavailable` | Queue send failed. The provider will retry, so watch first |
| Events accepted but no D1 rows | Consumer not deployed or bound, or `service-events` has the wrong consumer |
| DLQ growing | Poison message or a permanent downstream error |

For secret problems, see [Secret rotation](secret-rotation.md).

## When not to replay

Stop and investigate instead if any of these apply.

- **Signature failures from an unknown sender.** That is probing, not a lost event.
- **A refunded or disputed payment.** Check Stripe first. Replaying `succeeded` after a refund would start delivery for a refunded customer.
- **A cancelled booking.** `bookings.status = 'cancelled'` is terminal by design.
- **Data past its retention window.** Anything older than the retention or lawful-basis window for the contact.
- **An unfixed fault.** A deploy or configuration bug you have not fixed yet.

## Replaying safely

Consumers are idempotent, so a duplicate is skipped. That makes replay safe once the root cause is fixed. If it is not fixed, the consumer simply fails again.

1. **Prefer provider-side resend** for missed ingress (for example Stripe's "resend"). It re-verifies and re-normalises the event, and duplicates are harmless.
2. **Re-queue a DLQ message** only after the root cause is fixed.
3. **Replay in `occurredAt` order** where it matters. Cancel-before-create is handled, but keep it tidy.
4. **Reset a stuck ledger row only with intent.** Take a restore point and confirm the target first:

   ```bash title="Restore point (D1 Time Travel)"
   wrangler d1 time-travel info <DB_NAME>
   ```

   ```sql title="Confirm exactly one row matches"
   SELECT * FROM webhook_events WHERE id = 'evt_…';
   ```

   ```sql title="Reset, then re-enqueue the event"
   UPDATE webhook_events SET processing_status = 'received' WHERE id = 'evt_…';
   ```

## Duplicate events

Duplicates are expected and handled. A `duplicate` log outcome is normal.

Duplicate **side effects** are a bug: two workflows or two CRM contacts. Check `delivery_workflows.workflow_key` and the HubSpot email search.

## To confirm

Use this runbook when a provider reports failed deliveries, a booking or payment is missing, or a DLQ is growing. Work through triage, decide whether replay is safe, then replay in the least invasive way.

Triage

Check these four places in order.

  1. Provider dashboard. Delivery attempts and response codes (Stripe, Cal.com).

  2. Worker logs. Structured JSON, searchable by requestId, correlationId and eventId. Emails and tokens are redacted.

    wrangler tail --config apps/service-hooks/wrangler.jsonc

  3. D1. Look for events that never finished.

    SELECT processing_status, COUNT(*) FROM webhook_events GROUP BY 1;
    SELECT * FROM webhook_events
 WHERE processing_status != 'processed'
   AND received_at < datetime('now', '-15 minutes');

    received for a long time means a crashed or retrying attempt. failed means the system gave up.

  4. Dead-letter queues. service-events-dlq, crm-sync-jobs-dlq and client-delivery-jobs-dlq. Messages are kept only for the queue retention period, so triage promptly.

Symptoms and likely causes

SymptomLikely cause
Provider shows 400 invalid_signatureWrong or rotated secret, body modified by a proxy, or clock skew (Stripe)
500 webhook_not_configuredSecret not set for that environment
503 temporarily_unavailableQueue send failed. The provider will retry, so watch first
Events accepted but no D1 rowsConsumer not deployed or bound, or service-events has the wrong consumer
DLQ growingPoison message or a permanent downstream error

For secret problems, see Secret rotation.

When not to replay

Stop and investigate instead if any of these apply.

  • Signature failures from an unknown sender. That is probing, not a lost event.
  • A refunded or disputed payment. Check Stripe first. Replaying succeeded after a refund would start delivery for a refunded customer.
  • A cancelled booking. bookings.status = 'cancelled' is terminal by design.
  • Data past its retention window. Anything older than the retention or lawful-basis window for the contact.
  • An unfixed fault. A deploy or configuration bug you have not fixed yet.

Replaying safely

Consumers are idempotent, so a duplicate is skipped. That makes replay safe once the root cause is fixed. If it is not fixed, the consumer simply fails again.

  1. Prefer provider-side resend for missed ingress (for example Stripe’s “resend”). It re-verifies and re-normalises the event, and duplicates are harmless.

  2. Re-queue a DLQ message only after the root cause is fixed.

  3. Replay in occurredAt order where it matters. Cancel-before-create is handled, but keep it tidy.

  4. Reset a stuck ledger row only with intent. Take a restore point and confirm the target first:

    wrangler d1 time-travel info <DB_NAME>
    SELECT * FROM webhook_events WHERE id = 'evt_…';
    UPDATE webhook_events SET processing_status = 'received' WHERE id = 'evt_…';

Duplicate events

Duplicates are expected and handled. A duplicate log outcome is normal.

Duplicate side effects are a bug: two workflows or two CRM contacts. Check delivery_workflows.workflow_key and the HubSpot email search.

  2. DLQ and queue retention periods.
  3. Whether Cal.com retries failed deliveries (see Cal.com). :::

:::info[Lifecycle: planned]

## Purpose

`auth.rjmlaird.co.uk` is the identity and access boundary for protected services and automation. Its single responsibility is to establish who a caller is for services that need it.

It is not a public user directory, not a user database, and not a replacement for Cloudflare Access.

## At a glance

| Field | Value |
| --- | --- |
| Hostname | `auth.rjmlaird.co.uk` |
| Classification | Identity and access |
| Visibility | Restricted |
| Lifecycle | Planned |
| Evidence | Owner-stated; not verified in this repository |
| Catalogue | [Generated public service catalogue](../generated/subdomain-catalogue.md) |

## What it provides

- Authentication callbacks and session handling for protected applications
- Short-lived state for sign-in flows, such as OAuth state and PKCE verifiers
- Validation of sessions and access tokens
- Controlled logout and revocation markers
- A clear boundary between public services and protected operations

## Boundaries

- Public portfolio and reference-data APIs need no sign-in
- Private dashboards and administrative tools are protected with Cloudflare Access
- Webhooks are authenticated by provider signature verification, not by this service
- Booking and billing use provider-backed customer flows where possible
- It does not store plaintext passwords, long-lived provider credentials, or data that needs strongly consistent single-use or revocation semantics

## Access model

Cloudflare Access is the primary edge access-control layer for protected subdomains where configured. A request reaching a Worker is not authorised unless the Worker validates the Access assertion or applies its own authorisation.

Humans sign in through approved identity providers; the documented design is GitHub sign-in with an allow-list. Automated clients use Cloudflare Access service tokens, not interactive login.

## Security considerations

- Keep short-lived, low-risk state in key-value storage only; keep anything needing strong consistency elsewhere
- Scope the shared session cookie deliberately; see [Security, privacy and access](../../platform/governance/security-and-privacy.md)
- Store secrets as Worker secrets, never in Git

## Dependencies

- Cloudflare Access (Zero Trust)
- A Worker with key-value storage (owner-stated)
- An approved identity provider

How each service route moves from first contact to payment, which steps are manual, how return pages work and what is still to build.

Each route into the business has its own entry point and its own system of record. Only discovery calls and paid mentoring sessions are fully automated in the MVP. This page sets out the routes, the return pages and the work that remains.

## Journeys

| Route | Entry | Step 2 | Money | System of record |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Advisory: discovery | Direct Cal.com booking | Cal.com confirmation and reminders | None | Cal.com, then the HubSpot contact |
| Advisory: focused review | Short enquiry | Manual reply with scope and fee | **Manual:** private Cal.com link or Stripe payment link | Stripe, for payment |
| Teaching | Enquiry, with a safeguarding tick | Suitability reply; agreement shared | After the agreement, the same manual step | HubSpot deal |
| Mentoring | Direct initial conversation, or enquiry | Cal.com | Paid sessions through a billing `serviceId` | Cal.com and Stripe |
| Speaking and media | Detailed request | Review and reply | Agreed outside the portal | HubSpot |

Enquiry-only routes have no automated quote-to-payment step in the MVP. The reply is a human-review action, and a payment link sent by hand is reconciled by the existing Stripe webhook.

## Return pages

After checkout or booking, providers redirect the visitor to a static confirmation page.

| Source | Redirect target |
| --- | --- |
| Stripe | `booking.rjmlaird.co.uk/confirmation/?status=paid` or `?status=cancelled` |
| Cal.com | `?status=booked` |
| Forms | `?status=received` |

:::warning[The status parameter proves nothing]
`status` only changes the wording on a static page. Proof of payment comes from the signed Stripe webhook, never from the redirect.
:::

## Not yet built

1. **Intake receiver.** `POST /v1/intake/*` with Turnstile, Zod validation and a stored submission record. Until it exists the forms have no `action` and show "not connected yet".
2. **Route-to-service mapping.** A mapping from routes (`advisory`, `teaching` and so on) to `SERVICES` ids, Cal.com slugs and Stripe price environment variables. The current `SERVICES` catalogue is a placeholder.
3. **Marketing consent.** A separate, unticked checkbox, needed only if MailerLite is used.

## Booking portal styling

`apps/booking/src/styles/booking-portal.css` owns its layout tokens (`--bp-*`) and reads only colour, font and radius tokens from the site's `global.css`. Fonts are self-hosted through Fontsource. Route accents follow the brand: teal, amber, violet and coral.

:::warning[Token gotcha]
Do not read `--w`, `--m` or `--mb` as lengths. In `global.css` they are colours.
:::

## To confirm

:::note[To confirm]
1. How a payment made through a manually sent Stripe payment link, which carries no booking intent, is matched to a `payments` row and a HubSpot contact. Reconciliation of payments to bookings is not in the MVP.
2. Whether the safeguarding tick on the teaching enquiry is stored, and where.
:::

Private WebDAV attachment storage for Zotero. It is not a public file host.

# dav.rjmlaird.co.uk

:::info[Lifecycle: planned]
This service is planned. It is documented from its intended scope and has not been verified as deployed in this repository. Do not treat it as a live interface until the [catalogue](../generated/subdomain-catalogue.md) says it is active.
:::

## Purpose

`dav.rjmlaird.co.uk` is private WebDAV-compatible storage for Zotero attachment synchronisation. Its single responsibility is to store and serve those attachments to the approved client.

It is not a public file host, CDN, public API or general document-management system.

## At a glance

| Field | Value |
| --- | --- |
| Hostname | `dav.rjmlaird.co.uk` |
| Classification | Storage |
| Visibility | Restricted |
| Lifecycle | Planned |
| Evidence | Owner-stated; not verified in this repository |
| Catalogue | [Generated public service catalogue](../generated/subdomain-catalogue.md) |

## What it provides

- WebDAV-compatible storage for Zotero attachments
- The read, write, list and delete operations needed for synchronisation
- A stable hostname to configure in Zotero's sync settings

Zotero adds its own `/zotero` path to a WebDAV address, so the configured address should normally be the hostname root. See [Zotero's sync guidance](https://www.zotero.org/support/sync).

## Storage architecture

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  Z[Zotero desktop] -->|HTTPS WebDAV| D[dav.rjmlaird.co.uk]
  D --> W[Dedicated DAV Worker]
  W -->|read and write objects| R[(Private R2 storage)]
```

The Worker is bound only to the storage it needs. Nothing here is exposed publicly.

## Supported methods

Only the methods the approved client needs are implemented.

| Method | Use |
| --- | --- |
| `OPTIONS` | Capability discovery |
| `PROPFIND` | List and describe files |
| `GET`, `HEAD` | Read |
| `PUT` | Write |
| `DELETE` | Remove |
| `MKCOL` | Create folders |
| `MOVE` | Only if the client requires it |

Unsupported methods return an appropriate error. Operations outside the DAV root are rejected.

## Boundaries

This service does not:

- Provide any public browsing, indexing or download interface
- Publish content through [cdn](cdn.md) or expose it through [api](api.md)
- Act as the source of bibliographic metadata, which Zotero and any approved research workflow manage; it stores attachment files only

## Access model

Anonymous access is not allowed.

| Client | Approach |
| --- | --- |
| Zotero desktop | Dedicated WebDAV credentials |
| Browser | Denied, or protected by Cloudflare Access |
| Administrative automation | Cloudflare Access service token or narrowly scoped credentials |
| Public | Denied |

## Security considerations

- Require HTTPS for every request
- Keep storage private; never expose a public development URL
- Use a dedicated Worker, separate from the public API
- Hold credentials as Worker secrets, never in Git
- Never log bodies, file contents or credentials
- Enforce an attachment-size limit
- Return non-cacheable responses for private content
- Reject path traversal and anything outside the DAV root
- Monitor availability without exposing a listing

## Dependencies

- A dedicated Cloudflare Worker and private object storage
- Worker secrets for credentials

- [Security, privacy and access](../../platform/governance/security-and-privacy.md)

- [Adding or changing a service](../../build/adding-a-service.md)

# docs.rjmlaird.co.uk

## Purpose

`docs.rjmlaird.co.uk` is the public documentation for the digital estate: how the services fit together, how to use and operate them, and why decisions were made. Its single responsibility is to publish accurate, versioned documentation.

## At a glance

| Field | Value |

| Hostname | `docs.rjmlaird.co.uk` |
| Classification | Documentation |
| Visibility | Public |
| Lifecycle | Active |
| Evidence | Verified from a repository |
| Catalogue | [Generated public service catalogue](../generated/subdomain-catalogue.md) |

## What it provides

- Architecture, platform service and integration documentation
- Guides, tutorials and architecture decision records
- Versioned snapshots, diagrams and local search
- A generated reference table of services, built from the canonical catalogue (see [Generated public service catalogue](../generated/subdomain-catalogue.md))

## Boundaries

This site does not:

- Provide an API or fetch catalogue data in the browser; tables are generated at build time from committed files
- Hold secrets, credentials, private URLs or customer data
- Replace service repositories, which own their own code and configuration
- Guarantee that a documented service is live; check the lifecycle on each page

Public documentation is visible to everyone. Operational detail that would help an attacker map private infrastructure belongs in a private repository.

## Access model

Public and unauthenticated. GitHub Pages cannot set custom response headers, which limits security headers (see [Security, privacy and access](../../platform/governance/security-and-privacy.md)).

What the rjmlaird-services system does, which Workers and hostnames it uses, how this section is organised and what is not built yet.

`rjmlaird-services` is the private repository behind the commercial side of rjmlaird.co.uk. It takes bookings and payments, verifies the webhooks that Stripe, Cal.com and HubSpot send, records what happened, keeps the HubSpot contact up to date and hands new clients over for delivery. It holds no public portfolio data; that lives in `rjmlaird-api` (see [ADR-0003](../../platform/decisions/ADR-0003-separate-public-api-from-webhook-services.md)).

:::info[Status: In development]
This section is built from the repository's own documentation. It has not been checked against deployed configuration. The service catalogue is still a placeholder, the intake forms are not connected, and several launch tasks remain. See the [launch checklist](../../operate/launch-readiness.md).
:::

## What it does

1. A visitor chooses a service on the booking portal. Free sessions are handed to Cal.com; paid sessions go to Stripe Checkout through the billing Worker.
2. Stripe, Cal.com and HubSpot send signed webhooks to `service-hooks`, which verifies each one and puts a normalised event on a queue.
3. Private consumers record the booking or payment in D1, idempotently, and queue follow-up jobs.
4. `hubspot-sync` updates the HubSpot contact (one way only). `client-delivery` starts a delivery workflow once per confirmed payment.

Enquiry-only routes (focused reviews, teaching, speaking) deliberately have no automated quote-to-payment step. See [Customer journeys](customer-journeys.md).

## Components

| Worker | Role | Reachable from |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `service-hooks` | Webhook ingress at `hooks.rjmlaird.co.uk`. Verifies signatures, enqueues events. | Provider servers |
| `booking` | Service listing, booking intents and the portal pages at `booking.rjmlaird.co.uk`. | Browsers |
| `billing` | Creates Stripe Checkout Sessions. | Browsers |
| `stripe-consumer` | Sole consumer of `service-events`. Handles payment events and passes Cal.com events to `calcom-consumer` over an RPC service binding. | Queue only |
| `calcom-consumer` | Records bookings and cancellations. | Service binding only |
| `hubspot-sync` | Upserts HubSpot contacts from `crm-sync-jobs`. | Queue only |
| `client-delivery` | Starts and records client-delivery workflows from `client-delivery-jobs`. | Queue only |

:::note[Naming]
The repository is `rjmlaird-services`. The Worker behind `hooks.rjmlaird.co.uk` is called `service-hooks`. Despite its name, `stripe-consumer` also receives Cal.com events; it routes them to `calcom-consumer`.
:::

# Platform services

This section documents the services that make up the rjmlaird.co.uk digital estate. Each page states whether its service is public, restricted or internal, and whether it is active, planned, reserved or retired. Hostnames, visibility and lifecycle are held in the canonical catalogue; see the [subdomain catalogue](../../platform/governance/subdomains.md) and the [generated public service catalogue](../generated/subdomain-catalogue.md).

## Service groups

| Group | Services |
| --- | --- |
| Public services | [web](web.md), [docs](docs.md), [data](data.md), [api](api.md), [status](status.md) |
| Assets and content | [cdn](cdn.md), [dam](dam.md), [upload](upload.md) |
| Developer surfaces | [dev](dev.md), [apps](apps.md), [tools](tools.md), [labs](labs.md) |
| Integration services | [auth](auth.md), [mcp](mcp.md), [hooks](hooks.md), [booking](booking.md), [dav](dav.md) |
| Control plane | [master](master.md) |

## Boundaries at a glance

| Service | Does | Does not |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `api` | Serve public portfolio and estate catalogue data | Expose customer records, billing, uploads or tokens |
| `data` | Serve curated, attributed reference data | Accept writes or hold private data |
| `cdn` | Deliver approved public assets | Accept writes |
| `upload` | Accept controlled writes | Deliver public assets |
| `dam` | Govern media assets | Offer public browsing |
| `dav` | Store Zotero attachments privately | Act as a public host, CDN or document system |
| `apps`, `tools`, `labs` | Catalogue distinct kinds of work | Duplicate a record across catalogues |
| `auth` | Establish identity | Replace Cloudflare Access or act as a user directory |
| `mcp`, `hooks`, `upload`, `dav`, `dam` | Serve restricted purposes | Allow anonymous use |

## Reading the pages

- **Visibility:** public, restricted or internal. Restricted is the default for protocol, integration, ingestion and management services.
- **Lifecycle:** active means serving; planned means intended but not verified as deployed; reserved means the name is held; retired means withdrawn.
- **Evidence:** how the lifecycle was established. Anything other than a repository is unverified.

Shared rules are not repeated on service pages. See [Security, privacy and access](../../platform/governance/security-and-privacy.md), [Observability, status and incident response](../../operate/status-and-observability.md) and [Environments and deployment model](../../platform/governance/environments.md). How the booking, billing and webhook Workers fit together, where the trust boundaries sit, which Worker holds which secret and how delivery stays idempotent.

The services system is a set of small Cloudflare Workers joined by queues. Browser-facing Workers are kept separate from provider ingress, and both are kept separate from the private consumers that touch storage. This page explains that separation and the delivery guarantees that follow from it.

## System diagram

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  subgraph PUBLIC["Public (browser-facing, limited)"]
    V[Visitor] --> B[booking]
    V --> BI[billing]
  end
  subgraph INGRESS["Provider ingress (public, signature-verified)"]
    S[Stripe] -->|POST /v1/webhooks/stripe| H[service-hooks]
    C[Cal.com] -->|POST /v1/webhooks/calcom| H
    HS[HubSpot] -->|POST /v1/webhooks/hubspot| H
  end
  BI -->|create Checkout Session| S
  B -.->|handoff URL| C
  H -->|verified, normalised| Q1[("service-events")]
  subgraph PRIVATE["Private consumers (no routes)"]
    Q1 --> SC[stripe-consumer]
    SC -->|RPC service binding| CC[calcom-consumer]
    SC --> Q2[("crm-sync-jobs")]
    CC --> Q2
    SC --> Q3[("client-delivery-jobs")]
    Q2 --> HSY[hubspot-sync]
    Q3 --> CD[client-delivery]
  end
  subgraph STORE["Private storage"]
    D1[("D1 database")]
  end
  SC --> D1
  CC --> D1
  HSY --> D1
  CD --> D1
  HSY -->|contacts API| HUB[HubSpot]
  Q1 -. DLQ .-> DLQ1[("service-events-dlq")]
  Q2 -. DLQ .-> DLQ2[("crm-sync-jobs-dlq")]
  Q3 -. DLQ .-> DLQ3[("client-delivery-jobs-dlq")]
```

The D1 tables are listed in the [data model](../../build/reference/data-model.md).

## Trust boundaries

1. **Public API** (`booking`, `billing`). Browsers are untrusted. Routes and methods are allow-listed, CORS origins are explicit, request bodies are validated with strict Zod schemas and requests are rate limited. No stored data can be read through these Workers.
2. **Provider ingress** (`service-hooks`). A request is untrusted until its signature verifies over the raw body. The Worker holds only the webhook secrets and a queue producer: no D1, no provider API tokens.
3. **Private consumers.** No routes. They are reachable only through queues and one service binding.
4. **Private storage** (D1 and queues). Never exposed over HTTP. D1 holds no card data, no raw provider payloads and no email addresses.

## Least privilege

Each Worker is bound only to what it needs.

| Worker | Queues | D1 | Service bindings | Secrets |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `service-hooks` | Produces `service-events` | No | No | Stripe, Cal.com and HubSpot webhook secrets |
| `booking` | None | No | No | None |
| `billing` | None | No | No | `STRIPE_SECRET_KEY`, `STRIPE_PRICE_*` |
| `stripe-consumer` | Consumes `service-events`; produces CRM, delivery and DLQ messages | Yes | `calcom-consumer` | None |
| `calcom-consumer` | Produces `crm-sync-jobs` | Yes | No | None |
| `hubspot-sync` | Consumes `crm-sync-jobs`; produces its DLQ | Yes | No | `HUBSPOT_ACCESS_TOKEN` |
| `client-delivery` | Consumes `client-delivery-jobs`; produces its DLQ | Yes | No | None (adapter-specific later) |

Secret names and where to set them are in the [configuration reference](../../build/reference/service-configuration.md).

## Delivery semantics

Queues deliver at least once, so every consumer is idempotent.

- `webhook_events` has a unique constraint on `(provider, provider_event_id)`. An event already processed is skipped.
- Business state and the "processed" mark commit together in one transaction (`D1.batch()`).
- Downstream messages are enqueued **before** the commit. A crash can therefore duplicate a message but never lose one.
- Duplicates collapse through deterministic event IDs, the unique `delivery_workflows.workflow_key` and HubSpot's email-keyed upsert.
- Payments: `checkout.session.completed` and `payment_intent.succeeded` map to a single `payments` row. Delivery starts only on the first transition to `succeeded`.

Messages that exhaust their retries go to a dead-letter queue (DLQ), one per queue. See the [webhook failures runbook](../../operate/runbooks/webhook-failures.md).

## Admin interface (documented, not built)

Any future admin UI or API belongs in its own Worker behind Cloudflare Access (identity-aware, with SSO and MFA), on a non-public hostname, reading D1 through a read-only binding or a dedicated service binding. It must not be added to `booking`, `billing` or `service-hooks`.

## Not in the MVP

- Customer portal (it needs verified identity; `POST /v1/customer-portal-sessions` returns `501`).
- HubSpot inbound events (the webhook route verifies and acknowledges only).
- Reconciliation of payments to bookings (`payments.booking_id` is reserved).
- Booking reschedules.

## To confirm

:::note[To confirm]
1. Queue and DLQ retention periods, and who is alerted when a DLQ receives a message.
2. Whether one D1 database (plus a staging copy) is shared by the four consumers. The launch checklist implies this.
:::
