How content for rjmlaird.co.uk and docs.rjmlaird.co.uk is authored, validated and rendered, including the shared brand system and its known synchronisation gap.

Content across the ecosystem is written as plain files in Git, built into static pages and deployed automatically. This page explains the frameworks involved, how the two main sites share a visual identity, and where the content model is still undefined. ## Static site generation and frameworks | Site | Framework | Content source | Status | | --- | --- | --- | --- | | Main site (`rjmlaird.co.uk`) | Astro | To confirm (for example Markdown or content collections) | Live (owner-stated) | | Docs (`docs.rjmlaird.co.uk`) | Docusaurus 3.10.2 with React 19 | Markdown in `docs/` | Live (repository) | | Labs (`labs.rjmlaird.co.uk`) | To confirm | To confirm | Live (linked) | | Wiki (`wiki.rjmlaird.co.uk`) | Astro with server-side rendering | Notion, synced into D1 | Proposed | Two frameworks are in use deliberately. Astro suits a bespoke, design-led main site. Docusaurus provides navigation, versioning, search and Mermaid support for documentation without custom work. ## Docs content model (verified) | Element | Where it lives | | --- | --- | | Pages | `docs/**/*.md`, with front matter | | Navigation | `sidebars.ts`, which is explicit rather than generated | | Site settings | `docusaurus.config.ts` | | Landing page project cards | `src/data/projects.ts` | | Brand tokens and theme overrides | `src/css/custom.css` | | Diagrams | Mermaid code blocks inside Markdown | | Search | Local, client-side search plugin (no external search service) | | Language and locale | British English (`en-GB`) | | Licence | Documentation under CC BY 4.0 (stated in the footer) | A page is not visible in the sidebar until it is added to `sidebars.ts`. The build fails if any link points to a page that does not exist. ## Structured content and type validation Type-safe validation with **Zod** is used in the services code (the shared service contracts package, owner-stated). Whether the main site validates content with Astro content collections and Zod schemas is **not yet documented**. :::note[To confirm] - Whether the main site uses Astro content collections, and with which schemas. - Whether the CV, portfolio and research content have a structured data format, or are ordinary pages. - Where Zotero-derived research data is meant to surface on the site. ::: ## The shared brand system The main site's `src/styles/global.css` is the **single source of truth** for the brand: an ink, teal, amber and violet palette, with Space Grotesk, Inter and JetBrains Mono typography, designed to meet WCAG AA or better. The `rjmlaird-dev` project shares the same file. The docs site reproduces the brand in `src/css/custom.css` and loads the three fonts from Google Fonts. :::note[To confirm / technical debt] The docs repository's README states that `custom.css` holds **placeholder** hex values to be copied by hand from `global.css`. Until that is done, the two sites do not match, and every future brand change needs a manual copy. Candidate fixes, in order of effort: 1. Copy the values once and note the date here. 2. Publish the tokens as a small package or a single hosted CSS file that both sites import. 3. Generate both stylesheets from one tokens file. Also consider self-hosting the fonts. Loading them from Google Fonts makes a third-party request on every docs page view, which should be reflected in the privacy notice. ::: ## Content authoring and Markdown workflows 1. Write or edit Markdown (or MDX) on a branch. 2. Preview locally with `pnpm start`. 3. Open a pull request; CI typechecks and builds, failing on broken links. 4. Merge to `main`; the site deploys. ```mermaid flowchart LR author([Author]) --> md["Markdown or MDX
in Git"] md --> pr["Pull request"] pr --> ci["CI: typecheck, build,
link check"] ci -->|"pass"| main["Merge to main"] ci -->|"fail"| author main --> deploy["Deploy to host"] deploy --> live(["Live site"]) ``` ### Authoring notes for MDX Docusaurus parses `.md` files as MDX. Curly braces and angle brackets in ordinary prose are read as code, so put them in backticks or a code block. This is the most common cause of a failed docs build. ## Related pages - [Media, assets and CDN strategy](media-and-assets.md) - [APIs and integrations](apis-and-integrations.md) - [Naming conventions and standards](../governance/standards.md)

The shared brand system

The main site’s src/styles/global.css is the single source of truth for the brand: an ink, teal, amber and violet palette, with Space Grotesk, Inter and JetBrains Mono typography, designed to meet WCAG AA or better. The rjmlaird-dev project shares the same file.

The docs site reproduces the brand in src/css/custom.css and loads the three fonts from Google Fonts.

:::note[To confirm / technical debt] The docs repository’s README states that custom.css holds placeholder hex values to be copied by hand from global.css. Until that is done, the two sites do not match, and every future brand change needs a manual copy. Candidate fixes, in order of effort:

  1. Copy the values once and note the date here.
  2. Publish the tokens as a small package or a single hosted CSS file that both sites import.
  3. Generate both stylesheets from one tokens file.

Also consider self-hosting the fonts. Loading them from Google Fonts makes a third-party request on every docs page view, which should be reflected in the privacy notice. :::

Content authoring and Markdown workflows

  1. Write or edit Markdown (or MDX) on a branch.
  2. Preview locally with pnpm start.
  3. Open a pull request; CI typechecks and builds, failing on broken links.
  4. Merge to main; the site deploys.

Authoring notes for MDX

Docusaurus parses .md files as MDX. Curly braces and angle brackets in ordinary prose are read as code, so put them in backticks or a code block. This is the most common cause of a failed docs build.

The services behind rjmlaird.co.uk, how they are separated, the conventions they follow and the third-party systems they connect to.

The ecosystem exposes a small number of services, each with a single job. They run as Cloudflare Workers, share common conventions, and connect to a handful of third-party platforms. This page lists them, explains the separation between public and commercial systems, and records the conventions to follow.

:::info[Status: Draft]
Everything here is owner-stated. None of it has been checked against deployed configuration. The existing [API overview](../../build/api/overview.md) is still a template.
:::

## Public APIs and private operations

| Kind | Services | Rule |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Public, read-oriented | [api](../../catalogue/first-party/api.md), [data](../../catalogue/first-party/data.md) | Serve only content already approved for publication. No customer records, billing, private operations, raw uploads, access tokens or private data |
| Restricted | [hooks](../../catalogue/first-party/hooks.md), [mcp](../../catalogue/first-party/mcp.md), [upload](../../catalogue/first-party/upload.md), [dav](../../catalogue/first-party/dav.md), [dam](../../catalogue/first-party/dam.md) | Denied by default; each states its access model |
| Browser-facing integration | [booking](../../catalogue/first-party/booking.md) | A narrow boundary to providers; never exposes customer records |

## Service inventory

| Service | Hostname | Purpose | Visibility | Status |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `rjmlaird-api` | `api` | Public portfolio and content data | Public | Proposed (deployment to confirm) |
| `rjmlaird-services` | `hooks`, `booking`, `billing` | Verified webhook ingress; booking and checkout APIs; payment, booking and CRM workflows. See [Services](../../catalogue/first-party/index.md) | Machine-facing and browser-facing; private repository | In development |
| `rjmlaird-auth` | `auth` | GitHub sign-in with a user allow-list | Browser-facing | In development |
| Wiki | `wiki` | Private, read-only Notion-backed wiki | Private | Proposed |
| Zotero WebDAV | `dav` (intended; to confirm) | File sync for Zotero, plus a research ingest route | Authenticated clients | In development |

### Why public and commercial services are separate

The public portfolio API and the commercial webhook service are deliberately **different systems** (see [ADR-0003](../decisions/ADR-0003-separate-public-api-from-webhook-services.md)). The commercial service exposes no public portfolio data and no customer lists. The public API has no access to payment or CRM events. Neither can leak what it does not hold.

## Conventions

| Convention | Rule | Basis |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Framework | Hono on Cloudflare Workers, written in TypeScript | Owner-stated |
| Versioning | URL prefix `/v1/` | Webhook, WebDAV and research routes already follow it |
| Validation | Zod schemas, shared through a contracts package | `rjmlaird-services` |
| Documentation | OpenAPI for any API with external consumers | Zotero WebDAV spec exists; the docs template suggests generating from OpenAPI |
| Service-to-service calls | Cloudflare service bindings (for example the `AUTH` binding to `rjmlaird-auth`) | Owner-stated |
| Authoritative records | HubSpot stays the CRM authority; no bidirectional sync | Owner-stated |

## Known routes

| Route | Service | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `/v1/webhooks/stripe` | `hooks` | Verified payment events |
| `/v1/webhooks/calcom` | `hooks` | Verified booking events |
| `/v1/webhooks/hubspot` | `hooks` | Verified and acknowledged; enqueues nothing in the MVP |
| `/v1/services`, `/v1/booking-intents` | `booking` | See [HTTP contracts](../../build/reference/http-contracts.md) |
| `/v1/checkout-sessions`, `/v1/customer-portal-sessions` | `billing` | The portal route returns `501` |
| `/webdav` and `/v1/webdav` | WebDAV service | OPTIONS, GET, PUT and DELETE, tagged "WebDAV" in OpenAPI. Intended to live on [dav](../../catalogue/first-party/dav.md), not the public API |
| `/v1/research` | WebDAV service codebase | Zotero API ingest into R2 under `papers/` |

## Authentication patterns

| Surface | Mechanism | Status |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Interactive sign-in | GitHub OAuth through `auth`, with an allow-list of users | In development |
| Session | Cookie shared across `*.rjmlaird.co.uk` | In development |
| Private wiki | Cloudflare Access (initially one account) | Proposed |
| Webhook endpoints | Provider signature verification | In development |
| Public API | To confirm; at minimum rate limiting | To confirm |

See [Security, privacy and access control](../governance/security-and-privacy.md) for the trade-offs of the shared cookie.

## Webhook boundaries

1. Provider webhooks enter only through [hooks](../../catalogue/first-party/hooks.md). No other service accepts them.
2. A request is untrusted until its signature verifies over the raw body.
3. The gateway holds webhook secrets and a queue producer, never storage or provider API tokens.
4. Verified events are normalised into internal events; provider payloads are never passed on as they are.
5. A redirect or client claim is never proof of an event. Only a verified webhook is.

The contracts are in [HTTP contracts](../../build/reference/http-contracts.md) and [Internal events](../../build/reference/events.md).

## Contract and versioning rules

- Version the URL (`/v1/`) for HTTP APIs and the type name (`…v1`) for internal events.
- Additive, optional changes stay in the current version. A breaking change creates a new version, and the old one is removed only after every consumer has moved.
- Consumers send unknown event types to a dead-letter queue instead of dropping them.
- Money is an integer in minor units plus an ISO 4217 currency, never a float.
- Validate every external input with a schema.
- Publish OpenAPI for any API with external consumers.

| Stripe | Payment events | Inbound webhooks |

| Notion | Source content for the wiki | Outbound pull on a daily schedule |
| Zotero | File sync and library ingest | Inbound from clients |

The scheduled jobs, queue consumers and CI workflows that run without manual intervention, and the principles for building new ones safely.

Several parts of the ecosystem run without anyone pressing a button: a documentation build on every merge, queue consumers that react to payments and bookings, and a planned daily wiki sync. This page lists them and sets out how new automation should behave.

## Workflow inventory

| Workflow | Trigger | What it does | Status |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Docs build and deploy | Push to `main`; pull request build check | Typechecks, builds and deploys the docs | Live (repository) |
| Stripe event processing | Verified webhook, then queue | Records payment events | In development |
| Cal.com event processing | Verified webhook, then queue | Records booking events | In development |
| HubSpot sync | Queue consumer | Updates the CRM; HubSpot stays authoritative | In development |
| Client-delivery follow-ups | Queue consumer | Records a durable workflow once per confirmed payment and calls a handover adapter (the default adapter only logs) | In development |
| Wiki sync | Daily schedule | Pulls the chosen Notion page tree into D1 | Proposed (architecture agreed) |
| Zotero research ingest | Request to `/v1/research` | Stores library data in R2 under `papers/` | In development |
| Local scripts (data parsing, metadata extraction) | Manual | To confirm | To confirm |

## Design principles

These are proposed standards for any new automation:

1. **Verify before trusting.** Check the sender's signature on every inbound webhook before doing any work.
2. **Acknowledge fast, process later.** Accept the event, put it on a queue, return quickly. Do the work in a consumer.
3. **Be idempotent.** The same event arriving twice must not charge, email or record twice. Store a processed-event key.
4. **Fail visibly.** Failed messages should land somewhere you will see them, not disappear.
5. **One authority per record.** Never synchronise in both directions. HubSpot owns contacts; the automation writes to it.
6. **Run on a schedule only if you must.** Prefer manual or event-driven triggers for the first release. The wiki starts with a scheduled pull and no webhooks.

## Reference flow: payment or booking event

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
  autonumber
  participant P as Stripe or Cal.com
  participant H as hooks Worker
  participant Q as Queue
  participant C as Consumer Worker
  participant D as D1
  participant CRM as HubSpot

  P->>H: Signed webhook
  H->>H: Verify signature
  alt Invalid
    H-->>P: Reject
  else Valid
    H->>Q: Enqueue event
    H-->>P: Acknowledge
    Q->>C: Deliver message
    C->>D: Record event (idempotent)
    C->>CRM: Update contact
  end
```

## To confirm

1. Do any local scripts run on the owner's machine (for example for Zotero or metadata extraction), and what do they depend on?
2. Each services queue has a dead-letter queue (see the [webhook failures runbook](../../operate/runbooks/webhook-failures.md)). Who is alerted when one receives a message?
3. Who is told when a scheduled job fails?

ADR-0001: Docusaurus on GitHub Pages for the docs
The documentation site is built with Docusaurus and deployed to GitHub Pages through GitHub Actions.

:::info[Recorded retrospectively]
This decision was already implemented when it was written down. The original reasoning was not recorded, so the context below reconstructs it from the repository.
:::

## Status

Accepted.

## Context

The ecosystem needs a documentation site at `docs.rjmlaird.co.uk` that supports versioned documentation, search, diagrams and a custom domain, and that is cheap to run for a single maintainer. The services themselves run on Cloudflare Workers, but documentation is static content.

## Decision

Build the docs with Docusaurus (with Mermaid and local search enabled) and deploy them to GitHub Pages using GitHub Actions. The `docs` hostname points at GitHub Pages through a CNAME record.

## Consequences

- Hosting is free and tied to the repository. Deployment is automatic on a push to `main`.
- Broken links fail the build, which protects the quality of the site.
- GitHub Pages cannot set custom response headers, which limits security headers.
- There are no pull-request preview deployments.
- DNS is split between GitHub Pages and Cloudflare, so the [domain model](../domain-model.md) must document both.

## Alternatives considered

> To confirm: which alternatives were weighed at the time (for example another static documentation framework, or hosting the docs on Cloudflare). They were not recorded.

  • R2 storage and operations (writes and reads) are metered, while egress is not. Check the current free allowances and prices before planning bulk storage.
  • Set a calendar reminder to review usage quarterly.

Backup

R2 is durable storage, not a backup. The private research store holds data that is hard to recreate. To confirm: whether it has an independent copy, and whether a periodic sync to another bucket or provider is needed. Public assets should also exist in their source form (git or local originals).

DecisionOne public R2 bucket on one custom hostname, origin-pull via Cloudflare’s edge, with separate private storage
StatusProposed
Alternatives consideredGitHub Pages only (no cache control, no object storage); a separate image CDN or DAM (extra cost and maintenance); several subdomains (sprawl); exposing R2 via r2.dev (not for production)

CostsVendor concentration on Cloudflare, manual cache hygiene for mutable files, cookie-scope care on the shared domain

ADR-0002: Justify subdomains before creating them
A subdomain is created only if it needs a different runtime, security boundary, audience or external platform; otherwise content is delivered as a path.

## Status

Proposed.

## Context

The planning inventory lists 34 candidate subdomains, many of which overlap. Each real subdomain brings its own DNS record, certificate, deployment and navigation. Search authority is split across hostnames. Because the session cookie is shared across `*.rjmlaird.co.uk`, every subdomain also sits in the same trust zone.

## Decision

Create a subdomain only if it needs at least one of: a different runtime or build, a different security boundary, a different owner or audience with a distinct brand, or an external platform that requires it. Otherwise deliver the content as a path on the main site. Every subdomain must have an entry in the [subdomain catalogue](../governance/subdomains.md) with a status before a DNS record is added.

## Consequences

- Around 16 of the inventory hostnames become paths, and 5 are not created.
- One certificate, one navigation and one deployment cover most content.
- Some short URLs (for example `cv.rjmlaird.co.uk`) are lost unless a vanity redirect is added.
- Moving a section to its own subdomain later is possible, but needs redirects.

## Alternatives considered

- **One subdomain per topic** (the original inventory). Rejected: heavy maintenance, fragmented authority, and a larger shared-cookie surface.
- **No subdomains at all.** Rejected: the Workers services, docs and private tools genuinely need separate hostnames.

ADR-0003: Separate the public API from the webhook services
The public portfolio API and the commercial webhook and workflow services are separate systems with separate repositories and hostnames.

:::info[Recorded retrospectively]
This reflects a design stated by the owner. Deployment of both systems is not yet verified.
:::

## Status

Accepted.

## Context

Two kinds of service are needed. One serves public portfolio data to anyone. The other handles commercial events from Stripe, Cal.com and HubSpot, and updates customer records. They have different audiences, different security needs and very different consequences if compromised.

## Decision

Keep them separate. The public portfolio API lives in `rjmlaird-api` at `api.rjmlaird.co.uk`. Commercial operations live in the private `rjmlaird-services` repository, with webhook ingress at `hooks.rjmlaird.co.uk`. The services repository exposes no public portfolio data and no customer lists.

## Consequences

- A flaw in the public API cannot expose payment or CRM data, because it holds none.
- Each system can have its own rate limits, secrets and release cadence.
- There are two repositories and two hostnames to maintain.
- Shared concerns, such as sign-in, are handled by `auth` rather than duplicated.

## Alternatives considered

- **One combined API.** Rejected: it mixes public and private concerns and enlarges the blast radius of any fault.

ADRs record durable architectural decisions, including context, alternatives, the decision and consequences. General plans and implementation tasks belong in the roadmap or relevant build guide.

An architecture decision record (ADR) is a short note that captures one decision: why it was needed, what was chosen and what follows from it. Future maintainers should be able to read a record and understand the reasoning without asking the person who made it.

## When to write one

Write an ADR when a decision is hard to reverse, affects more than one system, or would puzzle a future reader. Do not write one for routine choices.

## Format

Each record lives in this folder as `ADR-NNNN-short-title.md` and has five sections: **Status**, **Context**, **Decision**, **Consequences** and **Alternatives considered**. Copy `_template.md` to begin.

| Status | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| Proposed | Written, under discussion |
| Accepted | In force |
| Rejected | Considered and declined |
| Superseded | Replaced by a later record, which it links to |

Records are never rewritten once accepted. Supersede them instead.

Who can reach what across rjmlaird.co.uk, how secrets and sessions are handled, and the privacy considerations that follow from the integrations in use.

This page describes the controls that protect the ecosystem and the data it handles. It separates controls that are known from those that are proposed, and it highlights the places where the architecture makes a trade-off that readers should understand.

:::warning[Not a compliance statement]
This page documents intended design. It is not a security audit, and it is not legal advice. Anything marked *To confirm* has not been checked.
:::

## Trust zones

| Zone | Examples | Who can reach it | Status |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Public content | Main site, docs, labs | Anyone | Live |
| Public API | `api` | Anyone, with rate limits | Proposed |
| Machine-facing | `hooks` | Verified third-party senders only | In development |
| Authenticated | `wiki`, any future tools | Allow-listed GitHub accounts | Proposed |

## Access control

| Control | Detail | Status |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Sign-in | GitHub OAuth through `auth`, restricted to an allow-list | In development |
| Private wiki | Cloudflare Access, initially one account | Proposed |
| Webhooks | Signature verification on every inbound request | In development |
| Public data | `hooks` exposes no portfolio data or customer lists | Owner-stated design |

## Estate-wide access rules

| Rule | Detail |
| --- | --- |
| Restricted by default | Protocol, integration, ingestion, management and operational services deny anonymous access unless their page says otherwise |
| Edge first | Cloudflare Access is the primary edge control for protected hostnames where configured. Workers still validate the assertion or apply their own authorisation |
| Machines are not people | Automated clients use service tokens or scoped credentials, never interactive sign-in |
| Least privilege | Each Worker is bound only to the storage, queues and secrets it needs |
| Public means curated | Public services serve only content approved for publication |
| Nothing sensitive in public docs | No secrets, account or binding identifiers, internal hostnames, bucket names, private URLs or exact access-policy rules |

## The shared session cookie

The design shares one session cookie across `*.rjmlaird.co.uk`. This gives single sign-on across the ecosystem, but it has a consequence that shapes other decisions: **every subdomain is inside the same trust zone**. Any page on any subdomain receives the cookie.

Practical rules that follow:

1. Never host or serve untrusted or user-generated content on any subdomain. This is why [upload](../../catalogue/first-party/upload.md) must be restricted, accept programmatic writes only and never deliver what it receives, and why `sandbox` is avoided.
2. Treat a compromise of any subdomain as a potential compromise of the session.
3. Keep the number of subdomains small, and keep the cookie `Secure`, `HttpOnly` and `SameSite`-restricted.
4. Prefer scoping cookies to the narrowest host that needs them wherever sign-in is not required.

:::note[To confirm]
The cookie's exact attributes, its lifetime, and how an administrator is revoked from the allow-list.
:::

## Secrets management

Secrets are named in documentation but never shown. Store them as Worker secrets, set them from standard input, rotate them on a schedule and on suspicion of leakage, and never place them in a repository, ticket, chat, catalogue or generated file.

- Secrets are held as **Cloudflare Worker secrets**, not in repositories (the wiki's Notion token is the stated case).
- The docs workflow needs no custom secrets.
- Dependencies are installed with `--frozen-lockfile` in CI, so builds use exactly the versions committed.

The services Workers hold their Stripe, Cal.com and HubSpot credentials as Worker secrets, split so that each Worker holds only what it needs (see the [configuration reference](../../build/reference/service-configuration.md)). Rotation is documented in the [secret rotation runbook](../../operate/runbooks/secret-rotation.md). Not yet documented: who holds recovery access.

## Edge security and headers

| Topic | Position |
| --- | --- |
| Transport security | HTTPS everywhere; see [Domain and DNS model](../domain-model.md) |

| Rate limiting | Required for any public endpoint; mechanism to confirm |
| Subdomain takeover | Mitigated by deleting DNS records when a service is retired |

## Privacy

The integrations in use process personal data: HubSpot (contacts), Stripe (payments), Cal.com (bookings) and the sign-in service (GitHub identity). The docs site also loads fonts from Google Fonts, which makes a third-party request from visitors' browsers.

The following should be reflected in a single privacy page at `/privacy` on the main site and linked from every site's footer:

1. What data each integration collects and why.
2. Retention periods.
3. How a person requests access to or deletion of their data.
4. Which third parties act as processors.
5. Whether any analytics or cookies are used.

## Threats to keep in mind

| Threat | Mitigation |
| --- | --- |
| Forged webhook | Signature verification and idempotency |
| Replayed webhook | Store processed-event keys |
| Leaked secret | Worker secrets; never commit; rotate on suspicion |
| Dangling DNS record | Remove records with the service |
| Compromised subdomain under shared cookie | Few subdomains; no untrusted content |
| Malicious dependency | Lockfile; review updates |

## To confirm

1. Are any analytics or error-tracking tools installed on any site?
2. What are the allow-list and revocation procedures for `auth`?
3. Are there security headers set on the main site?
4. Is two-factor authentication enforced on GitHub, Cloudflare, the registrar and HubSpot?

The shared session cookie

The design shares one session cookie across *.rjmlaird.co.uk. This gives single sign-on across the ecosystem, but it has a consequence that shapes other decisions: every subdomain is inside the same trust zone. Any page on any subdomain receives the cookie.

Practical rules that follow:

  1. Never host or serve untrusted or user-generated content on any subdomain. This is why upload must be restricted, accept programmatic writes only and never deliver what it receives, and why sandbox is avoided.
  2. Treat a compromise of any subdomain as a potential compromise of the session.
  3. Keep the number of subdomains small, and keep the cookie Secure, HttpOnly and SameSite-restricted.
  4. Prefer scoping cookies to the narrowest host that needs them wherever sign-in is not required.

:::note[To confirm] The cookie’s exact attributes, its lifetime, and how an administrator is revoked from the allow-list. :::

Secrets management

Secrets are named in documentation but never shown. Store them as Worker secrets, set them from standard input, rotate them on a schedule and on suspicion of leakage, and never place them in a repository, ticket, chat, catalogue or generated file.

  • Secrets are held as Cloudflare Worker secrets, not in repositories (the wiki’s Notion token is the stated case).
  • The docs workflow needs no custom secrets.
  • Dependencies are installed with --frozen-lockfile in CI, so builds use exactly the versions committed.

The services Workers hold their Stripe, Cal.com and HubSpot credentials as Worker secrets, split so that each Worker holds only what it needs (see the configuration reference). Rotation is documented in the secret rotation runbook. Not yet documented: who holds recovery access.

Naming rules for hostnames, repositories, Workers and routes, plus the page template, front matter, status labels and callout conventions for architecture documentation.

Consistent names and consistent pages make a sprawling ecosystem easier to navigate. This page records the naming conventions already in use, and the standards every architecture page must follow.

## Naming conventions

| Thing | Convention | Example |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Hostname | Lowercase, one label, describes a function | `docs`, `auth`, `hooks` |
| Repository | `rjmlaird-` followed by the purpose | `rjmlaird-docs`, `rjmlaird-auth`, `rjmlaird-services` |
| Worker service | Matches the repository or the app | `rjmlaird-auth` |
| API routes | Versioned prefix | `/v1/webhooks/stripe` |
| KV keys | Versioned prefix per service | `auth:v1:` |
| Environments | `development`, `staging`, `production` | `rjmlaird-services` plan |
| Monorepo layout | `apps/`, `workers/`, `packages/`, `migrations/`, `docs/` | `rjmlaird-services` |
| Documentation files | Lowercase, hyphenated | `domain-model.md` |
| ADR files | `ADR-NNNN-short-title.md` | `ADR-0001-docusaurus-on-github-pages.md` |

## Documentation standards

### Writing style

- Use clear, precise British English: optimisation, centralised, programme.
- Use sentence case for headings.
- Keep one idea per page; link rather than repeat.
- Capitalise system names consistently: Cloudflare Workers, Astro, Docusaurus, Zod, GitHub Pages.
- Prefer plain language, but include the technical detail a maintainer needs.

### Page template

Every architecture page uses this structure:

1. Front matter (below).
2. An introductory paragraph saying what the page covers.
3. A status admonition if the page is not fully verified.
4. Headings at `##` and `###` only.
5. Tables or lists where they help; short paragraphs elsewhere.
6. A **To confirm** section if anything is unverified.
7. A **Related pages** list.

### Front matter

```yaml title="Front matter"
---
id: page-identifier
title: Page title in sentence case
description: One sentence for search results and link previews.
sidebar_position: 1
status: Draft
confidence: Partly verified
last_reviewed: 2026-10-11
---
```

| Field | Values | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `status` | Live, In development, Proposed, Draft, Deferred, Deprecated | The state of the page's subject. Use **Draft** for pages that mix several subjects, and give per-item status in tables |
| `confidence` | Verified, Partly verified, Unverified | How much has been checked against a repository or configuration |
| `last_reviewed` | A date | When a person last checked the content against reality |

ADRs are the exception: their `status` is Proposed, Accepted, Rejected or Superseded.

The built-in "last updated" footer comes from Git history. `last_reviewed` is separate: it records when someone *verified* the page, not when it was last edited.

### Platform service pages

Each service under `docs/catalogue/first-party/` states whether it is public, restricted or internal, names one primary responsibility, says what it does not do and links to shared pages instead of repeating shared rules. Use only the headings that fit the service, for example "Public interface", "Access model", "Security considerations", "Storage architecture", "Catalogue model", "Monitoring model", "Protocol interface" or "Supported methods".

Front matter adds `visibility` and `lifecycle`, which must match `data/subdomains.json`; the generator fails the build step if they differ.

Never write credentials, secrets, account or binding identifiers, internal hostnames, bucket names or private URLs. Link between docs with relative file links ending in `.md`.

### Generated files

Files under `docs/catalogue/generated/` are derived. Mark them clearly, never edit them by hand, and regenerate them with `pnpm run docs:generate`.

### Status labels

Labels are defined in the [architecture overview](../overview.md#status-labels). Use them in tables as plain text, with the evidence in brackets where it matters, for example "Live (repository)".

### Marking uncertainty and technical debt

Use a note admonition with a fixed title, so they can be searched for:

```md title="Uncertainty callout"
:::note[To confirm]
What is unknown, and how to find out.
:::
```

```md title="Technical debt callout"
:::note[To confirm / technical debt]
What is missing or deferred, and the suggested fix.
:::
```

Never fill a gap with a plausible guess. If a provider, record, tool or setting is unconfirmed, say so.

### MDX caution

Curly braces and angle brackets in ordinary prose break the build because Docusaurus reads `.md` as MDX. Put them in backticks or a code block.

## Architecture decision records

Record any decision that is hard to reverse, affects several systems, or would puzzle a future reader.

- Store records in `docs/platform/decisions/`, named `ADR-NNNN-short-title.md`.
- Use the template at `docs/platform/decisions/_template.md` (a file starting with an underscore is excluded from the site).
- Every record has these sections: **Status**, **Context**, **Decision**, **Consequences** and **Alternatives considered**.
- Status is one of Proposed, Accepted, Rejected or Superseded.
- Never rewrite an accepted record. Supersede it with a new one that links back.

See the [ADR index](../decisions/index.md).

## Related pages

- [ADR index](../decisions/index.md)
- [Writing and versioning docs](../../start-here/contributing.md)

## Catalogue taxonomy

### Status

Status labels are defined in the [architecture overview](../overview.md#status-labels). The brackets after a status give the **evidence** behind it:

| Evidence | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| Repository | Verified from a repository's configuration |
| Owner-stated | Described by the owner, not independently checked |
| Linked | Referenced from another live site |
| None | Appears only in the planning inventory |

### Priority

| Priority | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| **Now** | Needed for the current build or already live |
| **Next** | Worth doing once the current work lands |
| **Later** | Reasonable, but not before there is content or demand |
| **Defer** | Postpone until a concrete requirement appears |
| **Merge** | Do not create; deliver as a path on another site |
| **Avoid** | Do not create; adds complexity without enough benefit |

### Category

**Content**, **Application**, **Infrastructure**, **Tooling** or **Services** (revenue-related pages).

## When a subdomain is justified

A subdomain earns its place only if it needs **at least one** of the following:

1. **A different runtime or build**, such as a Worker or a separate static generator.
2. **A different security boundary**, such as private access or untrusted input.
3. **A different owner or audience** with a genuinely separate brand.
4. **An external platform that requires it**, such as a SaaS custom domain.

Everything else becomes a path on the main site. Paths share one certificate, one set of search authority, one deployment and one navigation, so they are cheaper to run and better for search.

## Recommended simplification

Applying the justification rule above to all 37 entries gives this end state:

| Outcome | Hostnames |
| --- | --- |
| **Keep as subdomains** | `www` (with apex redirect), `docs`, `labs`, `space`, `research`, `api`, `auth`, `hooks`, `wiki` |
| **Add later if needed** | `status`, one asset host (`cdn` or similar) |
| **Defer** | `dev`, `courses`, `dashboards`, `mcp` |
| **Merge into paths** | `cv`, `portfolio`, `astro`, `talks`, `tutoring`, `physics`, `maths`, `mentoring`, `coaching`, `resources`, `stem`, `booking`, `bio`, `newsletter`, `privacy`, `images` |
| **Avoid** | `home`, `sandbox`, `dam`, `upload`, `app` |

### Why merge so many?

| Criterion | Effect of many subdomains | Effect of paths |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Maintainability | One build, deployment and navigation per subdomain | One build and one navigation |
| SEO | Search authority is split across hostnames | Authority accumulates on one host |
| DNS and certificates | A record, a certificate and a hosting target each | Nothing extra |
| Security boundary | Every subdomain sits under the shared session cookie scope, so a weak or untrusted one weakens all of them | Same boundary, but fewer surfaces |
| Branding | Visitors see a fragmented set of properties | One coherent brand |
| Long-term cost | Each is a permanent maintenance liability | Marginal |

### Service-offering pages in particular

`tutoring`, `physics`, `maths`, `mentoring` and `coaching` share one audience and one booking flow. A single `/services` section with a page per offering, and one booking link, is easier to maintain and ranks better than five separate sites. `resources` already has a sanctioned path alternative in the inventory, and should take it.

### Exceptions worth defending

- **`research`** is kept because it may carry its own build and data pipeline. If it turns out to be an ordinary set of essays, merge it into `/research`.
- **`space`** is kept because it serves a distinct audience and can carry a distinct identity. If it never grows its own navigation, merge it too.
- **`labs`** is kept because experiments carry unpredictable dependencies that should not share a build with the main site.

### Vanity redirects

A subdomain that only redirects (for example `cv` to `/cv`) is cheap to run but still needs a DNS record and a certificate. Create one only if the short address appears on printed or fixed material, and record it here.

## Changing the catalogue

Recommended simplification

Applying the justification rule above to all 37 entries gives this end state:

OutcomeHostnames
Keep as subdomainswww (with apex redirect), docs, labs, space, research, api, auth, hooks, wiki
Add later if neededstatus, one asset host (cdn or similar)
Deferdev, courses, dashboards, mcp
Merge into pathscv, portfolio, astro, talks, tutoring, physics, maths, mentoring, coaching, resources, stem, booking, bio, newsletter, privacy, images
Avoidhome, sandbox, dam, upload, app

Why merge so many?

CriterionEffect of many subdomainsEffect of paths
MaintainabilityOne build, deployment and navigation per subdomainOne build and one navigation
SEOSearch authority is split across hostnamesAuthority accumulates on one host
DNS and certificatesA record, a certificate and a hosting target eachNothing extra
Security boundaryEvery subdomain sits under the shared session cookie scope, so a weak or untrusted one weakens all of themSame boundary, but fewer surfaces
BrandingVisitors see a fragmented set of propertiesOne coherent brand
Long-term costEach is a permanent maintenance liabilityMarginal

Service-offering pages in particular

tutoring, physics, maths, mentoring and coaching share one audience and one booking flow. A single /services section with a page per offering, and one booking link, is easier to maintain and ranks better than five separate sites. resources already has a sanctioned path alternative in the inventory, and should take it.

Exceptions worth defending

  • research is kept because it may carry its own build and data pipeline. If it turns out to be an ordinary set of essays, merge it into /research.
  • space is kept because it serves a distinct audience and can carry a distinct identity. If it never grows its own navigation, merge it too.
  • labs is kept because experiments carry unpredictable dependencies that should not share a build with the main site.

Vanity redirects

A subdomain that only redirects (for example cv to /cv) is cheap to run but still needs a DNS record and a certificate. Create one only if the short address appears on printed or fixed material, and record it here.

How the canonical public service catalogue works, what each field means, when a subdomain is justified and how to change the catalogue.

Every hostname under rjmlaird.co.uk is registered once, in a machine-readable catalogue. Documentation, API discovery and status monitoring read that catalogue instead of repeating hostname facts by hand. This page explains the catalogue and its rules. The table itself is generated: see the [Generated public service catalogue](../../catalogue/generated/subdomain-catalogue.md).

:::warning[A row is not a deployment]
Lifecycle records intent unless the evidence is a repository. Check the **evidence** field and the service page before treating a service as live.
:::

## Canonical source

| Item | Location |
| --- | --- |
| Catalogue | `data/subdomains.json` |
| Schema | `schemas/subdomains.schema.json` |
| Generator | `scripts/generate-subdomain-catalogue.mjs` (`pnpm run docs:generate`) |
| Generated table | [Generated public service catalogue](../../catalogue/generated/subdomain-catalogue.md) |

The catalogue holds public, non-sensitive facts only. It never holds secrets, account or binding identifiers, internal hostnames, private management or health URLs, or access-policy detail. The generator validates the file, checks that each linked service page exists and agrees on visibility and lifecycle, and writes the table. Nothing is fetched in the browser or at build time.

## Fields

| Field | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `slug` | Unique lowercase label; also the service page name |
| `hostname` | Fully qualified hostname, or `null` for a concept |
| `purpose` | One public-safe sentence |
| `classification` | The service's single primary kind (below) |
| `visibility` | Who may reach it |
| `lifecycle` | Where it is in its life |
| `evidence` | How the lifecycle was established |
| `documentation` | Service page path, relative to `docs/` |
| `publish` | Whether the record appears in the generated public table |

| Visibility | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `public` | Anyone may read it |
| `restricted` | Authenticated or approved clients only; the default for protocol, integration, ingestion and management services |
| `internal` | Operational only; not normally listed in a public catalogue |

| Lifecycle | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `active` | Serving, verified or credibly stated |
| `planned` | Intended or in development; not verified as deployed |
| `reserved` | The name is held; nothing is built |
| `retired` | Withdrawn; redirect or remove DNS |

Classifications: `website`, `documentation`, `api`, `data`, `asset-delivery`, `asset-management`, `ingestion`, `identity`, `protocol`, `integration`, `storage`, `status`, `catalogue`, `developer`, `experimental` and `control-plane`. Evidence values are `repository`, `owner-stated`, `linked` and `none`.

## When a subdomain is justified

A subdomain earns its place only if it needs **at least one** of the following:

1. **A different runtime or build**, such as a Worker or a separate static generator.
2. **A different security boundary**, such as private access or untrusted input.
3. **A different owner or audience** with a genuinely separate brand.
4. **An external platform that requires it**, such as a SaaS custom domain.

Everything else becomes a path on the main site. Paths share one certificate, one set of search authority, one deployment and one navigation, so they are cheaper to run and better for search.

## How to change the catalogue

1. Edit `data/subdomains.json`. Do not edit the generated file.
2. Create or update the service page and keep its `visibility` and `lifecycle` front matter identical to the catalogue.
3. Run `pnpm run docs:generate`, then commit the regenerated table.
4. Record any non-obvious choice as an [ADR](../decisions/index.md).

The full checklist is in [Adding a service](../../build/adding-a-service.md).

:::note[To confirm]
Whether this repository owns the catalogue or a separate control-plane repository does. If another repository owns it, import a sanitised snapshot rather than keeping two copies; see [master](../../catalogue/first-party/master.md).
:::

Build, verify and deploy the Astro documentation site.

## Local verification

Use Node.js 20 or later and the pinned pnpm version in `package.json`.

```bash
corepack enable
pnpm install
pnpm validate
pnpm dev
```

## Release flow

1. Make changes on a feature branch.
2. Run content validation, internal-link checks, Astro type checks and the production build.
3. Review the generated site locally with `pnpm preview`.
4. Open a pull request and review the rendered pages, metadata, navigation and links.
5. Merge only after CI passes.
6. Confirm the deployment and custom domain after release.

## Rollback

Revert the faulty commit and redeploy the last known-good revision. Verify the site and sitemap after rollback. Confirm the actual hosting workflow before using this runbook in production.
